CENSUS IN ROCK ISLAND
speechtext:
1.	What is the name of the party who is taking the census in Rock Island, Quebec?
2.	Does he live in Canada or the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CENSUS IN ROCK ISLAND
speechtext:
1.	Mr. J. W. Downing.
2.	Mr. Downing is a Canadian, bom in the county of Comipton; his place of business and his post office address are at Rock Island, P.Q. At this point there is one community known as "The Three Villages" made up of Stanstead and Rock Inland in the province of Quebec and Derby Line in the state of Vermont. The entire population forms one community and the same churches, schools, moving picture theatres and railway station are used by the entire population. For example there is an ice skating rink at Derby Line, a roller skating rink at Stanstead, a golf course at Stanstead, an Odd Fellows hall at Derby Line, a Masonic lodge at Stanstead, and an opera house half in Rock Island and half in Derby Line. The public library is also situated on the line as well as the buildings of some of the residents,

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY
TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY
speechtext:
1.	Has an arrangement been arrived at between the Ontario government and the federal government that three survey parties would go over the ground this season to study the routing of the trans-Canada highway in northern Ontario?
2.	What was the nature of the arrangement between the Ontario and the federal governments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY
speechtext:
It is hardly possible to
answer this question with a mere yes or no. I can only say that the Ontario government has suggested that they were sending survey parties over the ground of what might possibly be the routing of the completion of a trans-JCanada highway through northern Ontario. The only arrangement made was that, that suggestion having been made, this government stated that it would be very glad if such a survey were proceeded with. That is as far as it went.

UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext:
1.	Has Premier Henry or any other member of the Ontario government requested or suggested assistance from the federal government for unemployment relief for the coming winter 1931-32?
2.	Has the Minister of Agriculture for the province of Ontario requested or suggested assistance from the present federal government in bringing about better conditions for the marketing of farm produce?
3.	Has any member of the Ontario government requested or suggested assistance from the present federal government in the construction of a trans-Canada highway through the province of Ontario?
4.	Has any member of the Ontario government requested or suggested that the present federal government should undertake the full payment of old age pensions in the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext:
It would hardly be satisfactory, perhaps, to the hon. member who asks this question if it were answered merely with a yes or no. With respect to the first question the answer would be this:	It has
been suggested that the arrangements made last year be continued or improved upon so far as the province of Ontario is concerned. With respect to the second question, some verbal suggestions have been made. The answer to the third question would be yes. With respect to the fourth question there is no very definite information available, but it is believed that suggestions were made that the federal government should discharge the payment in full of old age pensions as soon as possible.

CANADIAN BANK DEPOSITS
speechtext:
1.	What is the total of deposits in all the banks of Canada?
2.	What is the total amount of loans outstanding from all the banks of Canada?
3.	What percentage in actual money do the banks have in relation to the total amount of money loaned by them?
4.	How much money do the people of Canada owe the mortgage companies, loan companies. banks and insurance companies?
5.	What is the amount of the national debt of Ca nada ?
6.	What is the amount of gold, silver bullion, and paper money in circulation in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN BANK DEPOSITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a rule
the hon. gentleman is very considerate in the questions he asks. The information sought in this instance however is contained in the Canada Gazette and in various other publications which are supplied to members of parliament. One of the sections of the question however is not thus answered and, from any information in the hands of the government, cannot well be answered. I refer to part 4 which is as follows:
How much money do the people of Canada owe the mortgage companies, loan companies, banks and insurance companies?
That information of course is not in the possession of the government. Many of the mortgage companies are incorporated under provincial charters, and such information is not available to the federal government.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are proceeded with I desire to mention a matter that was brought to the attention of the house yesterday by the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly).
To-day is the sixty-fourth anniversary of confederation, and it is not unusual on a day such as this that we pause and look back upon our past, take stock of the present, and look forward to the future. So far as the past is concerned I think we can contemplate it with some degree of satisfaction and pride. The achievements of the Canadian people have, I think, been unrivalled in the history of the world by any people so few in number and inhabiting so vast an area. So far as the future is concerned we contemplate it with great courage and hope and confident faith.
But with respect to the present it is undoubted that practically a national calamity has overtaken a portion of our country. In days gone by this parliament has voted very-considerable sums of money to assist others who have been deprived of their homes or who have suffered from great calamities when they were not citizens of our own Dominion or of our own empire. At the moment it is clear from the information the government has received, and is receiving, that in consequence of lack of moisture and of great heat a very considerabe portion of the province of Saskatchewan and smaller portions of the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba will not this year produce a crop. In some areas this is the third successive year in which no crop has been produced, in others it is the second, while in the smaller areas it is the first year that such a calamity has overtaken them. The estimates vary as to the area affected. The commercial and agricultural editor of the Manitoba P'ree Press, Miss Cora Hinds, has completed a survey of the province of Saskatchewan, and by questionnaire, of the other provinces with respect to the grain crop, and it is now quite clear that

Farm and Unemployment Relief
notwithstanding the copious rains of the last thirty-six hours it will not be possible for any harvest in the way of grain to be reaped in a very substantial area.
The government of the province of Saskatchewan being primarily responsible for relief measures for those directly affected, is carrying on a survey, and the results of that have, in part, been communicated to this government. It is believed that within a very short time all the relevant information will be in our possession, but it is clear that the tremendous heat has not only affected the possibility of the continued life of live stock over a substantial area, but that 5,000,000 acres of land have been adversely affected so far as crop is concerned, and probably more.
Under those circumstances parliament has never been hesitant in granting relief by way of financial and other assistance to countries beyond our borders when such a disaster has overtaken their people, and before this house rises it is the purpose of the government to submit to parliament a measure that will, we believe, at least in part, show the desire and purpose of the Canadian people to assist those who are less fortunate than the inhabitants of other parts of Canada at this particular crisis in their history.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION
speechtext:
The extent to which that assistance will extend, depends, it is needless to say, upon the character of the information disclosed as the facts are more fully ascertained, but that it is tremendously serious goes, I think, without question, and I fear that perhaps it is the greatest national calamity that has ever overtaken this country. I hope that my fears are groundless, but I am confident from the information that has been given us that at least 100,000 people are directly affected, and their herds as well.
Obviously it has a direct bearing on the problem with which it will now become intimately associated, that of unemployment, and when dealing with this matter it is the intention of the government, after we have disposed of the business on the order paper and such other measures as we have to consider, to submit to parliament measures that we hope will enable us successfully to grapple with that difficulty during the coming winter and the balance of the year that is before us.
I think I could not do more than say that notwithstanding these disquieting symptoms of the manifest difficulties that must confront any government charged with responsibility at this time in connection with these and allied matters, the faith and confidence
that we have in our country is in no sense shaken, and although the trials and tribulations we face may be many and varied, we still have the confident belief that with the resources of our country and the perseverance and courage of the people we will be able to work out our manifest destiny upon the northern half of this continent. For that purpose I trust that whatever may be our beliefs politically, we may cooperate not only in rendering assistance to those stricken in the provinces, in the manner in which I have indicated, but in endeavouring to take care of the other situations which have developed in this country by reason of universal conditions prevailing throughout the world.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the country shares the profound regret of this house that a condition has arisen in western Canada of the serious character to which my right hon. friend has just referred, and I am equally sure the country will receive with satisfaction, as this house has received it, the assurance just given by the Prime Minister that the seriousness of this condition is fully appreciated by the administration and that the government is taking care to provide the necessary measures to meet it satisfactorily.
Referring to the introductory remarks of my right hon. friend, may I say that I share his view both as to the past and the future of this country, a past which has been very great and a future which we hope and believe will be greater still. I share his regret that the present is not what we would like to see it and I appreciate, and in fact have said all along, that the reason conditions in Canada are not as we should like to see them is in the main the result of a world condition. However, there has unhappily been added to that condition this, which I imagine is peculiar to our own country, of the serious damage which has been done the crops in a portion of western Canada.
My right hon. friend has spckem of the desirability of cooperation in a great national emergency such as the present. May I say to him that this cooperation will be given in the fullest measure and with the most hearty accord by all hon. members on this side of the house. I hope that if we venture to make one or two suggestions, my right hon. friend will not feel that those suggestions are made in a critical way, but rather as something which it is believed will be helpful and in its nature constructive.
In that regard may I say to him that it is now apparent that very large sums of
3248	COMMONS
Farm and Unemployment Relief
money will have to be spent this year to take care of the national calamity to which we are now referring, and that further sums will have to be spent in connection with unforeseen unemployment which may occur during the latter part of this year and throughout the coming winter. That being so, again I should like to suggest to my right hon. friend that he and the administration consider carefully the advisability of the immediate establishment of a national relief board, or something of the kind. I am not giving it any particular name, but I do wish to emphasize that I believe the matter is sufficiently important, and the amount of public expenditure sufficiently large, to warrant the government taking into its own hands, from a federal point of view, the administration of such funds as may be necessary for these relief purposes. At the time of the great Halifax disaster the government of the day appointed a relief commission to administer the 820,000,000 voted for purposes of relief. I imagine 820,000,000 will not begin to meet what the administration will have to spend in connection with relief matters this year, so I suggest that the administration very carefully consider the advisability of appointing a national board which will face this situation as a national emergency and a national obligation and become responsible, through the minister, to this parliament for the expenditure of public money from this federal source.
May I enlarge upon that suggestion to this extent, that I think such a scheme should include provincial boards and municipal boards in the larger municipalities, with which the national board could cooperate. The giving of public money to provinces or municipalities to spend in connection with their particular needs and obligations is not, to my mind, in the light of the experience we have had thus far in these matters, helping the situation; rather it is tending to aggravate it, and therefore I suggest to my right hon. friend and the members of the government that they consider very carefully this suggestion, which I am sure must have presented itself to their minds already.
I have just one further word to say in conclusion, and which I hope will not occasion a discordant note; as this is July 1, perhaps as my hon. friend has indicated, the day may assist us to come together in agreement on some matters which are of the past, particularly with respect to further discussion of them in the future. Hon. gentlemen opposite are now taking the view, I think correctly, that in relief matters the obligation is first a municipal obligation and in the next place a

provincial obligation, becoming a national obligation only when one or more of the provinces themselves represent to the Dominion that they are not in a position to cope with the situation as they find it within their own borders. That is the position of the administration of the day; that was the position I took more than a year ago, as leader of the administration, when sitting where my right hon. friend is sitting to-day. At that time, when I made the reference I did make to not giving a five cent piece to a province, hon. members wild see if they will look at the text in that regard that my remark was solely with respect to provinces that had not asked for any relief, that were not asking for relief at that time and that, in the circumstances, I felt were not entitled to any federal assistance simply because of certain demonstrations occurring then on this side of the house. I made that statement to-day in the hope that if hon. gentlemen opposite do not accept my word at the moment, a reference to Hansard will be sufficient to revise their views.
In conclusion may I repeat, Mr. Speaker, what I have already said as to the extent to which it may be possible for me personally to cooperate with the Prime Minister in helping to cope with this great problem. I shall feel it not only a duty but a great pleasure and privilege to be permitted to cooperate in in any way, and what I say of mysedf in that respect I say on behalf of all hon. members on this side of the house in regard to our cooperation with hon. gentlemen opposite in facing a matter of great national concern.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the crisis confronting this nation at the present time I think it is incumbent upon some member of the group in this corner of the house, representing as we do directly at least a portion of the area so badly affected and of the people who are suffering, to say a word on this occasion. In the absence of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) my colleagues have asked me to undertake this task.
May I first express our profound appreciation of the attitude of the Prime Minister at this time. I think perhaps at no time since assuming his high office has he more fuliy demonstrated his capacity for fulfilling its onerous functions that he has done to-day in giving full and complete recognition to the nature and the extent of the calamity which has overtaken a part of this great country. When the Prime Minister asks this house for its cooperation, it is perhaps unnecessary for

Farm and Unemployment Relief
me to say how gladly we in this corner will accept that invitation and cooperate to the fullest extent in our power in that good work. Coming into this house as we do, holding many views which are not held by some members, we have at least this in common: we are here for the definite purpose of offering, and of giving the fullest possible cooperation in any matter of this kind when it is in our power so to do. Without going into details- for this is hardly the time or the place to discuss details as to the management of the work -I need only say, speaking for ourselves, and on behalf of the suffering farmers we represent, that we appreciate the recognition of the situation which has been manifested in the helpful and encouraging attitude of the Prime Minister, and we shall be glad now and at any time to give our cooperation and assistance with a view to having these good wishes carried into effect.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION
speechtext: As representing a grouip, even though a very small group, in this house, I feel bound to say a word in regard to unemployment. It was very satisfactory indeed to learn that the Prime Minister intends to give us a statement before the close of this session with regard to this important matter. I would just urge one thing-the urgency of the need. 'Possibly some of us who have, been very closely connected with the unemployed realize their needs more fully than some others, and I would point out that an absolute demoralization is taking place at the present time across this country. It seems to me that work ought to be provided-remunerative work-in the immediate future, and I would welcome any such suggestion as that made by the leader of the oppositon, that an emergency committee be appointed at once and relief works of a constructive nature on a large scale undertaken without delay, so that a large number of transients might be taken off the road and that the homes of the people might not be broken up, which is a real danger at the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION
speechtext:
May I point out that the policy suggested by the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition is one that involves questions of very great legal magnitude. These difficulties have become extremely grave by reason of recent decisions of the privy council. The method suggested is one that has been engaging the attention of the government for the last few months, and my right hon. friend is perfectly correct when he says that no doubt this matter has suggested itself to the government. It has.
But I should like the attention of the exMinister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and of those members of this house who are of the legal profession, and I ask them to reflect for a moment just what our powers may be in dealing with matters that are primarily within the jiirisdictidn of the provinces. The late Lord Haldane observed that the provinces were quasi-sovereign entities, and in dealing with questions of relief we can do so only at the request and with the consent of the provinces affected. But, this not being war time, when we endeavour to appoint a committee which would have jurisdiction to enforce its edicts or its will, there is a constitutional difficulty of the first magnitude. And the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has just touched upon the fringe of one of them. What about those who, offered work, will not take it but demand that they be maintained? That has happened already. I am bound to say that in my judgment it is part of a studied propaganda that does not emanate within Canada. But that is not a matter of importance at the moment. If any hon. gentleman within sound of my voice, who has given thought to this matter, has any suggestion to make and will send it to me either by note or otherwise, it will be greatly appreciated. For just how the forces may be coordinated and sufficient power vested in a central body to see that the policies and conclusions arrived at are made effective is a matter that is certainly not free from great doubt.
The Minister of Justice has been giving it careful consideration and attention for weeks. I pointed out, in answer to one of my hon. friends yesterday, that one of the provinces had said it required no assistance in dealing with the problem of unemployment. With respect to the making of grants, there is no difficulty; with respect to the controlling of their administration, there is considerable difficulty. The extent to which a committee set up by this parliament to function in every province, except under conditions that might make its operations more or less useless, is a matter that might engage the attention of many of our friends. One of my friends, when I discussed it with him, said, "The answer is simple: no one will object". Well, knowing as I do something of what is transpiring in Canada, I am perfectly certain that not only will objections be registered but that action will be taken that will involve the expression of opinions by courts. And courts must administer the law regardless of the fact that emergencies exist, unless parliament makes a declaration of a character which it

may be very difficult for it to make, inasmuch as one of the provinces, as I have said, has intimated that it desires no assistance in dealing with the problem in question. I mention this because it seems to me to be the thresh-hold of all our consideration of this matter.

As the matter now stands the. resolution has the effect of raising the sales tax from one to 4 per cent, and a number of articles which were previously taxed at the full rate have been added to the exemptions from the sales tax. As I indicated last night there was provision made for "articles and materials for the sole use of any bona fide hospital when purchased in good faith for use exclusively by the said hospital, and not for resale." There were exempted from tax a certain limited number of articles under tariff items 476 and 476a. This makes it perfectly clear that when ' articles are purchased at a high cost for the

I also intimated last evening that another item had been added, namely that there would be a division of fence posts from round to split, because of a difficulty which had arisen in practice with respect to split fence posts.
Another item was added concerning articles purchased in Canada for the use of the Governor General. In practice no sales tax has been paid on these articles, and the officers administering the department desired that they should be added so that there would be no question as to the correctness of the procedure followed. Then there was a further item concerning item No. 695a of the customs tariff, -'"Paintings in oil or water colours, and pastels valued at not less than $20 each; painting and sculptures by artists domiciled in Canada but residing temporarily abroad for purposes of study, under regulations by the minister." When the budget was brought down on June 1 a number of items which were exempt from sales tax under the previous administration were placed at four per cent. I notice by the amendment of last night that these items are now exempt. I refer particularly to implements used in the fishing industry-gasoline	engines for fishermen,
engines of all kinds for the industry, vessels, boats and dories and other implements necessary for the prosecution of the fishing industry. I understood the Prime Minister to say last night, in answer to a question, that while the government had reversed their policy with regard to this matter, as a result I presume of the widespread agitation in Canada, it was impossible to pay back the sales tax to anyone who had paid it since June 1. May I point out to the Prime Minister and the Alinister of National Revenue, with respect to some of these items, that it would be a very simple matter to have the money refunded. If it is good policy to reverse what the government proposed to do on June 1, then I say that wherever it is possible to do so the money should be paid back to those who have paid it in. Take the sales of gasoline engines or engines for the use of fishermen. These engines go direct from the manufacturer to the fishermen. The manufacturer has a complete list of his customers, and he knows to whom he has sold engines s'ince June 1. There is no question about it, that, under the policy of the government, the manufacturer of gasoline engines had to add the four per cent to the price of the engine and the fishermen had to pay the amount. In such a case there would be no difficulty whatever in the Department of National Revenue refunding to the fishermen the extra amount paid by them, which payment the government now admits is not good policy. The same thing applies to the building of vessels and motor boats and dories. In Nova Scotia last year contracts were entered into by the shipbuilders of that province, mostly with American citizens, for the construction of $5,000,000 worth of vessels or yachts. These contracts were made prior to the bringing down of the budget by the present government. In figuring the prices of these vessels, the builders did not know, of course, anything about the sales tax. If these vessels were completed and launched at any time from June 1 until yesterday when the change was made, the shipbuilder
Special War Revenue Act

had to pay to the Department of National Revenue four per cent on the contract price. Clearly this involves a hardship on the shipbuilder. If he had a contract for, let us say, $45,000 on a vessel, he would not have anticipated this four per cent sales tax inasmuch as there was an exemption under the previous government. He entered into a contract to build that ship for someone, either in the United States or in Newfoundland, where practically all of our business in Nova Scotia is done, and he was compelled, under the budget of June 1, to pay into the treasury of this country $1,800, which was practically his profit on the transaction. In view of the fact that this four per cent was paid by the builder of the ship to the government, there should be no difficulty in tracing the person to whom the refund is due, and I submit that the government should arrange to pay back to the shipbuilder the amount w'hieh he had to pay in. He could not collect this four per cent from the man-

The hon. Minister of Fisheries last night moved a resolution whereby certain items are exempted from the one per cent excise tax. In the budget brought down on June 1 the excise tax was imposed upon all goods coming into Canada, and I desire to deal with one of the four items mentioned in the resolution brought down by the hon. Minister of Fisheries, carrying out the wishes of his leader, the Prime Minister. The resolution asks the house to exempt fish and other products of the fisheries of Newfoundland. While perhaps I would suffer more than a good many people from the effects of a tax of this kind, because for some thirty years I have been buying fish from Newfoundland, in view of the protests made by the fishermen's associations all over Nova Scotia during the last

twelve months, I would like to know why this particular item has been exempted from the excise tax. I would like to know also why it is necessary to exempt fish caught by fishermen in vessels registered in Canada or owned by any person domiciled in Canada. If I know anything about the high seas, and some people say I know a good deal more than I do know-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Than the hon. member
lets on.
-it seems to me that when a Canadian vessel catches fish .on the high seas, those fish are Canadian fish whether caught on the Grand banks of Newfoundland, the Sable Island banks, the Brown banks,-
The Royal bank.
-the Royal bank or the Bank of Montreal, which is my bank. I do not see why this item should be included.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have intimated already to the hon. member for Aniigonish-Guysborough that so far as we can ascertain -the returns will be made a few days hence- there are very few items which could give any concern at all, and with respect to those an order in council will be passed refunding the money so paid.
With respect to the second matter, I think the hon. gentleman knows better than any of us that there is a long-standing convention between Newfoundland and Canada. While it might be incorrect to speak of it as being an absolutely legal or binding obligation, I do not think any government would care to disregard it. The late government did not disregard it, and I am certain that this government will not. This convention provides that Newfoundland fish shall come into Canada free from any tax, and it is to give effect to the provisions of this long-standing convention that this item is included in the resolution. I am advised that this convention has been in force for some thirty or forty years.
There is another matter to which the hon. member has directed attention, namely, fish caught by fishermen in vessels registered in Canada or owned by any person domiciled in Canada, and the products thereof carried from the fisheries in such vessels. No one knows better than my hon. friend that at various times we have had discussions with respect to the modus vivendi of placing taxes upon fish landed from vessels of Canadian registry or boats that stopped at ports for the purpose of transhipment, and matters of that kind. It was abundantly made clear that any fish caught upon any of the banks to which the hon. member has referred, either

Special War Revenue Act
[DOT]within or without the three or twelve mile limit, shall be exempt from this tax, because such a catch is the result of the effort of the individual made beyond the territorial limit of our country, but made by a vessel which is Canadian, either by registry or by ownership by any person domiciled in Canada. "Domiciled" is a very difficult word to define. As we in the legal profession say, it involves the absence of any intention to go to some other country to live. It is to meet the very situation to which the hon. member referred that these fish are made free of this tax.

Mr. Chairman, in my opinion
it would never do to put a tax of any kind, whether it be an excise tax or otherwise, on fish coming in from Newfoundland, because of the fact that our fishing vessels must go to Newfoundland for their bait. We have had different examples of retaliation, and if a tax were put on fish coming in from Newfoundland, I have no doubt that the Newfoundland government would immediately tax our vessels on the bait which they must purchase in Newfoundland and which they can purchase nowhere else. In other words, the deep sea fishing of Nova Scotia would be ruined if these fish were not exempt from the tax, and I hope my hon. friend the Minister of Fisheries will give me credit for which I have just said.
I took up with the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of National Revenue a question which is of great importance at the present time to Nova Scotia. Under the Canada Shipping Act vessels over a certain tonnage must have masters possessing a certificate. These fishermen start to work sometimes as young as twelve years Of age. They go out first as threatens, and then as headers, then as splitters, and then they go into the dories as steersmen, and in working up from throater to captain they do not have an opportunity to acquire a sufficient education, nor have they the time to spare from their vocation to attend a navigation school and take the necessary examination for a captain's certificate. Under the present act the captain of a vessel over a certain tonnage, not possessing a certificate, cannot clear that vessel from port. During the war Canada lost practically all of her shipping due to the legislation with regard to this matter. At that time the ships in Nova Scotia practically transferred from Canada either to Newfoundland or the Barbados, where they allow a captain to sail a vessel without a certificate provided he is capable of doing so.
Last year a splendid new type of fishing schooner was built, but when that boat was measured by the surveyor of shipping it was found it was over-tonnaged, and the result is that the captain must get someone else to clear his boat. These boats are cooperatively owned, one man owning one Share, another a half share, and another two shares and so on; all the shareholders being fishermen, or members of their families. I took up this matter with the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of National Revenue and I would like to have some information so that I can telegraph to the people in Lunenburg who manage this vessel whether or not this vessel, owned in Nova Scotia and manned by Nova Scotians, can bring her fish into Nova Scotia free of duty and excise tax.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member has
raised a question which is covered, as he perhaps knows quite as well as I, by the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act. That act imposes upon us certain very distinct limitations which will be removed by the statute of Westminster. In other words, the power to pass sections of the Canada Shipping Act will be unlimited after the legislation we were discussing yesterday shall have been enacted by the imperial parliament. But may I say to my hon. friend that the issue which he raises is not limited to fishermen alone. I can show him on the statute books of this country in the various provinces legislation that allows a man to practise law without having passed the requisite examination, and there is at least one case of a gentleman being permitted, by act of the legislature, to practise medicine. In other words, there is a recognition of the principle that a certain measure of experience plus certain limited other qualifications which do not come up entirely to the examination requirements set by the bar association or the medical association shall be taken as sufficient. What my hon. friend has suggested is that that principle should be applied to others. You have young boys going to sea in fishing vessels. They go out upon the banks and work their way up until they are able to become mates and finally masters, but the statute says that they shall not clear those vessels from a port if the tonnage of the ship is greater than the limited tonnage mentioned in the statute; I think it is set at 100 tons.
One hundred and fifty tons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, it is 150 tons now In other words, if a ship by the measurement
Special War Revenue Act

of the registrar of shipping has a greater tonnage than 150, it must have a certificated master. That is a question which succeeding governments have had to consider in connection with lawyers and dentists and doctors and other professions, and it has been felt that a certain standard must be set and that that standard must be maintained. With respect to men who acquire their ability to handle ships from what you might call experience, without ever having passed examinations, there was until recent years a much wider latitude allowed, but as the statute now stands an uncertificated mariner cannot clear a ship in excess of 150 tons. I think I have put it correctly. The question of changing that cannot come up under this statute. It is, however, a matter of first-rate importance, which will have to be considered when the authority of this parliament to deal with the Merchant Shipping Act is complete and unrestricted. But as it stands I cannot see that it will affect this, because if my hon. friend will be good enough to look at the wording of the sales tax exemption, he will see that there is an absolute freedom from the excise tax of the catch, which is the important thing, that is, the fish taken by the mariner on the high seas, on the banks or elsewhere, if it is done in a registered Canadian ship. The other case mentioned by my hon. friend is also dealt with; that is the case of the vessel on the register of Barbados or the Bahamas, or some other country, manned by one domiciled in Canada.
And owned in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it is both owned and domiciled. My hon. friend will find that on page 8. That meets the case to which my hon. friend refers.
Are there two distinctions there? Would that mean, first, fish caught by vessels registered in Canada, and secondly, owned by persons domiciled in Canada? If it means that, it is satisfactory.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no doubt that there are the two classes. I think it is meant to cover the case my hon. friend has in mind.

I now have the information which I did not have when I spoke before. I find that I gave the wrong use for the poison. I thought it was for the destruction of grasshoppers, but I find that it is for the destruction of weeds. I have here a letter from the secretary of the Saskatchewan

portion of the letter which gives the names of the commodities. I see that Atlacide 's the name of the commodity that is used for the destruction of weeds.
