speechtext: If these items were not subject to the sales tax prior to the 1st of June, they are not now. I will look the matter up and ascertain definitely whether the items are in the exempted list.
I think they are not exempted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend from Kindersley that if they are not exempted, provision will be made accordingly.

I thank the Prime Minister for that statement. The letter which has been written to me by the secretary of the association states that the four per cent sales tax has been imposed since the early part of June, while prior to that it had not been.

I should like to revert to the question of canned vegetables. In looking through the act I find that schedule III on page 11 refers to vegetable plants and other farm produce sold by the individual farmer of his own production, also to fish and products thereof. Would that include canned salmon? Would the same interpretation of the act as was given to my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi apply in this case, where the words "other farm produce" are used? Would

Special War Revenue Act
that include also the cooperative societies? Many of the fanners in the province of Quebec unite to form a cooperative society and they manufacture canned fruit and canned vegetables of various kinds.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. frined will
observe by page 11 that vegetables, fruits, grains and seeds in their natural state, and so forth, are all free from this tax, and it also provides that other farm produce sold bv the individual farmer of his own production is exempt. I take it that bees, honey, sugar and so forth, if of his own production, will be free from the sales tax if he sells them. I have no doubt that that would not apply to the cooperative societies as it now stands. As the statute now stands the cooperative enterprise would be liable to a tax of two per cent.
Fish and products thereof are produced by the cooperative societies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are in exactly the same position.
They are exempt?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, they are exempt.

So that this schedule III
on page 11 would apply only to those who canned their own vegetables at home?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I would like to call to
the attention of the Minister of Finance conditions in the lumber business in British Columbia. Probably a different condition exists there than in any other portion of Canada. Many of the loggers manufacture logs and sell them to the saw mills. I have been unable to find wherein those logs produced by loggers will be exempt from this sales tax. The loggers would be paying sales tax, and then the lumber manufacturer who ' purchases the logs would also be paying a sales tax when the lumber is sold by him. Does the schedule provide for relief in respect to that situation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I assure my hon. friend
from Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury) that the tax will not be payable twice with respect to the same commodity.
Who will pay it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It will be paid once and
once only. The question as to who shall pay it will be determined by the language of the exemption. My hon. friend will observe on page 11 of the bill that logs and round unmanufactured timber are exempt.
I think that refers only to farmers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Oh, no, that refers to
everyone. There are "logs and round unmanufactured timber; British and Canadian coin and foreign gold coin; split fence posts; fence posts, railroad ties, pulpwood, tan bark and other articles the product of the forest, when produced and sold by the individual settler or farmer." That does not refer to logs and unmanufactured timber, but refers to other articles following. In practice, no tax has been collected heretofore, and that is a reenactment in that regard of the provisions which previously existed.

I should like to refer
again to the item of yeast as it appears on page 20 of the bill. I understand the Minister of Finance referred to it a minute ago He said that yeast was used in Canada in large quantities for purposes other than that of bread making. Would it be impossible to separate the yeast used and give exemption to that part which is used for bread making?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In view of the very large exemptions accorded in connection with all the products used by the baker in the manufacture of bread it was felt that yeast might reasonably be subjected to half of the sales tax. I think on consideration my hon. friend will admit that such a tax is no hardship, because yeast after all is not a very large item in the manufacture of bread.

I wish to ask a question in
reference to spraying and dusting material-covered by tariff item 219a as it appears at page 13 of the bill. Those articles have been exempt from sales tax. They were taken out of the list of exemptions on June 1 and have now been placed back in the list of exemptions. My point is this: In the Annapolis valley a large quantity of these dusting and spraying materials are used in the month of June, and as I understand the situation the dealers in these spraying and dusting material-added the sales tax to any they sold during that month. I am not sure about that, but I fancy it is the case. Presumably the returns will be now made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Shortly.

I believe they are to be made .by July 1. They will not have, to pay the government anything by way of sales tax. Is there any way of protecting the persons who bought spraying and dusting materials?
32m
Special War Revenue Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The question is perfectly clear; they should have the money refunded to them.
By the dealer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. When the returns come in we will see to it that an attempt is made to have that done.
All right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is only fair and proper that it should be done.

Following that up, and directing the attention of hon. members along the same line I wish to point out to my right hon. friend that the matter referred to by my hon. friend would be of a very serious nature and could not be governed by order in council. My right hon. friend suggested to the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) that where the tax under the original budget proposals has already been paid in connection with a vessel an order in council could be passed making a refund. I know of cases, however, as I am sure every hon. member does, in which goods have been actually purchased by the consumer. The consumer has paid the retailer, and quite possibly the retailer has made and will make no return. It will be difficult to get the money back. I wish to comment particularly upon articles in connection With which I feel very strongly, namely articles used by fishermen in connection with their work such as rope, head ropes for fishing nets, and fishing nets themselves. These are articles necessary for the outfitting of fishermen and in connection with which they have paid the dealer an amount equivalent to the regular price of the articles plus the increased sales tax. I submit to my right hon. friend that there must be some way of giving the money back to those, consumers. To my mind it is not fair that they should have to pay. The money has gone into the pockets of the wholesalers, or probably has gone another step farther, namely into the coffers of the government. I suggest that the government should not keep that money. Simply because those people happened to be outfitting at a particular time of the year is no reason why they should have to pay that money. Householders who have gone into stores and purchased cereals, ice cream, meats, salted or smoked, or any similar articles which were taken off the exemption list, upon which the sales tax of 4 per cent was imposed and which are now back on the exempted list, should not have to pay that money. I realize

my hon. friend will have some difficulty, and I do not think the difficulty can be overcome simply by saying that an order in council will be passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not suggest it could.

I understood my hon.
friend to say that the difficulty would be easily overcome because there were only a few cases involved. May I say to him that there are hundreds, perhaps thousands, of cases thoughout Canada.
Following the remarks of my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough I wish to refer to a matter which I do not think has been touched upon. In the town of Shelburne, in my own constituency, a yacht was being built and was being finished in June. Budget resolutions were brought down which imposed a sales tax of 4 per cent, and in addition a special excise tax of 5 per cent. When the owner came to get his register from the Department of Customs in the month of June he found he could not get it unless he paid something like $2,000. I do not know whether or not that amount has actually been paid to the department, but I submit this is a case upon which one could place his finger as indicating how far the budget resolutions went with regard to an industry in the province of Nova Scotia. That is a case where through the new budget resolutions about 9 per cent was being charged.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
know any cases where the money was paid?

No. I have brought the matter to the attention of my right hon. friend to indicate to him the burdensome nature of the tax that was being imposed. I am very glad I am now in a position to bring the matter to the attention of my right hon. friend and to ask that if any money has been paid a refund be made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Shelburne-Yarmouth will recall that five daya after the first of June the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryokman) made a statement with respect to the method of collection, the effect of which was more far-reaching than the mere statement itself. I am informed by the officials of the department that although the returns will not be made until the next few days, few, if any, complaints have been received of payments having thus been made. I will consider whether it may not be desirable to add to the bill a section declaring that any moneys paid with respect to such cases as that mentioned shall be returned to

Special War Revenue Act
the person from whom it was recovered. I wholly agree with my hon. friend that an order in council would have no effect in such a case, but I was directing my attention to the order in council which refunded money under the general law of the country to the person who paid the $1,700 or $1,800 mentioned by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough. We are wholly in accord with respect to the incidence of this legislation, and if my hon. friend could think of it in those terms as well as my hon. friend from Hants-Kings (Mr. Usley), and would prepare a declaration that would be ample to protect the rights of those who have paid, I should be very glad to have it. Ajt the moment as a matter of fact, we have received no information on the subject; I inquired this morning. That may be because time has not sufficiently run to enable complaints to reach us.

Has my hon. friend received any communication from the universities and colleges with regard to the exemption of chemicals used for educational purposes only? I have received a communication from Queen's university on the subject, but I cannot satisfy myself whether or not such chemicals are exempt.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would not that depend upon each chemical that is used?
That is why I should like to get the information. I see that "preparations" are mentioned. What would preparations be?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am told the word is construed to cover everything that has to be used' in connection with educational work. Whatever the construction has been heretofore it will be continued, for the same officials are continued.

That will be satisfactory,
because from the last communication I have received I would say these chemicals had been exempted before.
I understand fruits and vegetables to 'be free from the tax. What about the packages in which they come?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I mentioned last evening, Mr. Chairman, and there will be found in the bill, a special item dealing with coverings. I am quoting from page 12:
Usual coverings to be used exclusively for covering goods not subject to the consumption or sales tax; materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture of usual coverings to be used for covering goods not subject to the consumption or sales tax.

I would urge the Prime Minister to include canned vegetables in the exemptions from sales tax. I notice it was said to-day that canned fish are exempt, and on page 13 I notice that prepared cereal foods in packages are also exempt. This being so, it seems to me to be only logical that canned vegetables should be exempt. I believe they are just as necessary an article of food as canned fish or cereal in packages. Will the Prime Minister seriously consider their exemption? I think it is really improper to tax them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will take the matter under consideration. I cannot give an answer until I ascertain what is involved.

Just one other question. Can the Prime Minister tell us whether arsenic is exempt? It is used chiefly for poisoning grasshoppers. The matter was mentioned a little while ago. I am unable to find it in the bill. If the Prime Minister has not the information I would ask him to look into it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I understand it is exempt, but I will satisfy my mind on the point.

I may say it is exempt, because I was preparing to attack my right hon. friend on this very item. I may say he removed a good deal of the opposition that I had to the sales tax provisions in the budget when he restored the large exemption list. I am bound to say, however, that I scarcely understand the attitude of mind of hon. gentlemen opposite, who a year or two ago were going to abolish the sales tax altogether. Now they are in office they have to resort to a very stiff increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We will abolish it before we go out of office.
Well, we came very near abolishing it.
Another promise.

I would advise my hon. friend not to be too rasih in making such a promise now. I think my right hon. friend will find it very difficult, if not almost impossible, to trace the gales of goods throughout the past month in the price of which the sales tax has been included, in order that he may be able to return the sales tax so collected. Hon. gentlemen opposite take every occasion to point out how cautious the Liberal leader had been in bringing down legislation, but a little caution on the part

Special War Revenue Act

of hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to this matter would be very helpful as well. I think the rather unfortunate incidents the other day with respect to glass would not have occurred had a little caution been exercised by them. As a former member of the treasury board, may I say that I pressed very hard to have those exemptions made, they grew year by year as succeeding budgets were brought down under the Liberal regime, and naturally I did not want to see the present government lay violent hands upon the list. When you get the tariff increases coupled with the wiping out of the sales tax exemptions you hit very hard the people who must of necessity pay both taxes and are the least able to bear them. I want to congratulate my right hon. friend on his afterthought in now deciding to introduce by way of amendment the complete list, with one or two exceptions, of the exemptions from sales tax that we put into effect. When we come to the tariff items I shall voice a very strong protest against some of the increases, as they are most extraordinary, particularly in view of the fact that at the September session the government clothed themselves with very large powers to deal with the fixation of prices.

I notice calcium chloride is
subject to the 4 per cent sales tax. In view of the circumstances confronting the government I agree it may be necessary that this tax should be collected from individuals; but the provincial governments buy very large quantities of this article for laying road dust. I think my right hon. friend might very well take into consideration exempting provincial governments from payment of the sales tax where they buy calcium chloride direct.

I notice the
maritime provinces are using a great deal of this material now; the government of Nova Scotia has just placed an order for $90,000 worth. They are going to try it out on their roads to see if it will lay the dust, and the province of Prince Edward Island is considering trying it also.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman
sure it is calcium chloride? I will see what the item means in dollars and cents and let the hon. gentleman know.

This is used to lay the
dust on gravel and dirt roads, and costs in Canada between $27 and $32 a ton. The government of New Brunswick last year spent between $100,000 and $110,000 in connection 
with this work. I believe machinery used by governments for road purposes is exempt from sales tax, and this would come under the same classification.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I should like to ask my right hon. friend a question with regard to the excise tax of 1 per cent. The clause reads:
.... there shall be imposed, levied and collected a special excise tax of 1 per cent on the duty paid value of all goods imported into Canada.
If I recollect aright, when my right hon. friend was speaking on this matter he said this 1 per cent would apply to goods coming in free. Is that correct, or is it not? As this item reads at present I do not see how goods coming in free could be subject to the 1 per cent tax, because they have no duty paid value. On the other hand I should be sorry if goods which come in free at present should be made subject to this 1 per cent tax, because there must be very strong reasons for free importation, reasons which undoubtedly will affect the cost of living of many people, and which will affect also the industries of the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I had intended that this tax should apply to all importations. As it stands now it applies to the duty paid value of goods imported into the country, as the hon. gentleman has said. I do not recall, looking at the returns since it became operative, but my memory is that it has not been collected on free goods. However, I will satisfy myself on that point, perhaps during the dinner recess, and advise the right hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I should like
if it does not apply to duty-free goods to emphasize once more the importance of leaving the resolution as it is, because I am sure there must be very good reasons why certain goods come in free. Those reasons would apply to an excise tax just as strongly as to the customs tax.
Then I should like to ask my right hon. friend a question in regard to the proviso that the sales tax shall not apply to goods the duty paid value of which does not exceed $25, when imported by mail or express. As my right hon. friend knows, there is a good deal of travelling back and forth between this and other countries, and sometimes people bring in articles of trifling value. Is it the intention that the sales tax should be imposed on all articles brought in during the course of travel, or will this $25 exemption apply to articles of small value brought in by people

Special War Revenue Act
*who may be passing through the United States say by motor and returning to Canada from that country, or returning after a visit of any kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I explained last evening the idea is to render free of the excise tax goods valued at $25 or less brought in by mail or express. By the way, this is not the sales tax proviso; this has to do with the excise tax. As I explained last evening, when articles valued at $25 or less come through by express or mail they go upstairs in the customs house and very often are assessed a nominal duty.
I am frank to say that the question of the imposition of the tax on articles brought into the country by individuals had not entered into my thought at the moment, for the reason that usually the customs officers have exercised a very wide discretion in connection with small valuations, because of the fact that in the United States goods are exempt to the value of $100. Articles valued at $15 or $20 usually have come in without question, but I understand they are liable to the excise tax and, if the entry is made, they would have to pay the tax as it stands at the moment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think
there should be a definite understanding on that matter. For example, an hon. member might be called suddenly to spend a day in New York and in his hurry to get away forget to take with him his pyjamas and tooth brush. He would on his return have to pay an excise tax on both those articles if he brought them back. Surely in emergencies of the kind some reasonable discretion should be allowed.
Then may I ask my hon. friend another question:	Can he give to the committee any
idea of the amount of revenue likely to be foregone as a result of restoring these exemptions under the sales tax?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I promised last evening
that this morning I would inquire into that matter. Speaking broadly and generally it may be said that each one per cent of the sales tax has produced approximately $20,000,000. Last year the total was $20,783,944.15, but that was a poor year. In the previous year, when the rate was two per cent, the sum total was $44,858,751.22 and the year before, when the rate was 3 per cent, the amount collected was $63,646,671.22. In the previous year, however, when the rate was four per cent, each one per cent returned approximately $18,000,000. That was a very bad year; the total amount collected was $72,100,244.12, and in the years preceding that, each one per cent produced something less 22110-207J
than $20,000,000. The officers of the department are unable to state with any degree of authority what the changes in the exemptions will mean in dollars, but it will be a substantial sum of money running into some millions of dollars in any event. I am told it will be impossible to make any estimate of the exact sum. We budgeted on the assumption that each one per cent of the sales tax would produce something between $18,000,000 and $20,000,000. Before the third reading of the bill I will give the committee a statement of the amount received for the month of June. I will not have the revised figures, but to-morrow morning the figures will be available with respect to June, and I will give them to the committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I feel certain there will be general satisfaction that these exemptions are continued. They were made in the first instance because the articles concerned were largely in the nature of necessaries of life, or articles that affected the basic industries and the implements and instruments of production used in their development.
Doubtless now my right hon. friend will have to consider ways and means of making good some of the revenue he has lost in this connection, -and I should like immediately to make a suggestion to him in order to give him an opportunity to consider it before we proceed with some of the other resolutions. I suggest that my right hon. friend consider the advisability of restoring the graduated rate of tax formerly imposed on incomes in excess of $24,000. I feel sure that if he will do that he will receive from the public at large an appreciation equal to that which will be felt in connection with his action in restoring what formerly were exemptions under the sales tax.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will deal with that
matter when it is reached. The largest income from the sales tax was in the year 1923-24, when the amount collected was $100,990,076.80.
Has the minister made any estimate or has he any definite idea as to what additional revenue he will receive from the restoration of the excise stamp tax on cheques under ten dollars?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The officials of the department find it difficult to make an estimate, with respect to certain matters the tax was removed toy order in council. The officials inform me that it is quite difficult to give any certain information in regard to the matter. After the tax has been in operation a month or so they will be able to give a definite
326S
Special War Revenue Act

statement. It is just possible that we shall not 'be able to do it before the house rises because it does not become effective until the first of July. I am sorry I cannot give a more definite answer.

This is a tax to which personally I have been always opposed. It is a nuisance tax and nothing else. So far as I am concerned, I was always in favour of wiping out altogether the tax on cheques, and I am sorry that it was retained. Although I admit the necessity for revenues, I regret that the Minister of Finance has seen fit to restore that tax, making it in degree even worse than it was before. I would criticize that one provision in his budget as much as anything else. Its removal would be appreciated not only by business men but by those who issue small cheques and who find it a definite burden. And certainly it is a good deal of a nuisance. I would very much rather have seen this revenue raised in some other way and the nuisance tax on cheques wiped out. I can see no logical reason for placing a stamp tax on cheques. There are two principles of taxation that should be observed: one is a tax for service received, and the other a tax because of the ability of the taxpayers to pay. I do not think this tax is in accordance with either principle. Certainly there is no service received by the man who pays the tax on the cheque nor does it necessarily follow that because a man issues a cheque he has great ability to pay. There are very many people who issue cheques by reason of the nature of their business and who are not particularly wealthy or able to pay. It is in my opinion as had a tax as the old tax on window glass, on the panes of glass a man had in his bouse. I have not received very much sympathy in my objection to this tax, and so far as I was concerned I always argued against it in toto. I wish that the former administration, having partly removed it, had wiped it out altogether. It is a retrograde step now to widen the application of the stamp tax. I had hoped that the minister would be able to say how much revenue is obtained from the added tax, but I can understand, from a knowledge of the work of the department, that it is difficult to get such information. I have every sympathy with the Minister of Finance in his endeavour to get as much money as he can, but because this tax is based on no definite principle I must oppose it. It is simply a matter of reaching out and taking money where you can get it, but there is no principle upon which it rests. Moreover, it certainly involves a great nuisance from which the people might have been relieved.
[Mr. Bennett.1

On a former occasion I
brought up the question of the stamp on cream cheques, and I asked whether the Minister of Agriculture had been able to impress upon the Minister of Finance the desirability of exempting those cheques.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The question asked by
the hon. member (Mr. Brown) and that raised by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) touch the same matter-the imposition of a stamp tax on cheques. The tax in this country is 2 cents. In England it was a penny halfpenny and now twopence halfpenny, or perhaps it is only twopence. The fact is that this tax does represent a service rendered by the state to every person who issues a cheque. A cheque is drawn upon a bank, and a bank is the creation of the Dominion parliament, which assumes certain obligations with respect to safety, by supervision and inspection-

Why not tax the bank?
'Mr. BENNETT:	It is taxed-I am coming to that-and taxed heavily too.
Not in this way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
A distinct service is rendered by the state to all those who issue cheques-a service in the way of the preservation of law and order, and the maintenance of freedom of action in relation to all matters involved in commercial transactions. This is not a nuisance tax because there is provision made that postage stamps may be used instead of the excise stamp, and when you can use either you cannot describe it as a nuisance. But what is more important is that the embossed cheque in every country in the world is practically taking the place of the stamp which is affixed by an adhesive.
I do not think there is anything that brings home to the people better the importance of some measure of thrift and economy than a small tax on cheques. With respect to the cream cheques to which my hon, friend ha3 referred, may I say this. Under this list of exemptions the farmers are practically exempt from all forms of taxation. I may misjudge my fellow Canadians engaged in farming, but I do not believe there is one who will not be glad to make a contribution of 2 cents on every cheque in order to help this country to discharge enormous responsibilities of a financial character which it has to bear ,by reason of the calamity to which I referred this afternoon. That is my conviction; and
1	believe that many people who issue these small cheques will realize, as they affix that
2	cent stamp, that they are making some contribution to the revenues of the country.

Special War Revenue Act
I care not how small it is, there is nothing better for this country than that everyone should feel that he or she is taking some part in maintaining our institutions and providing the money which is required. It may be said that the sum involved is insignificant. Well, it is small. Take the cream cheque: the stamp represents perhaps 10 cents a week, $5 a year. And as I go about the country, afterwards receiving letters from people from whom I should little expect to receive them in these difficult times, I find that many of them, instead of asking to be relieved from this taxation, take this view: "Well, we think it is pretty hard, but we are glad to do our part." I have never seen a better spirit of cooperation manifested anywhere than I have observed in the letters I have received in respect to these matters. If there is one tax that can be justified it is that small tax on every cheque issued, and I venture to think that as time goes on no government will want to remove it. It will be recognized to be what I have said, an indication of willingness on the part of the people to make a real contribution, however small, to the wellbeing of the state and the maintenance of its institutions. If the tax has done one thing more than any other, it has made the people more curious as to how their money is being spent, and more insistent upon a strict accountability on the part of those who spend it. In time it will no longer be regarded as a nuisance tax but as one of very beneficial effect.

* The Prime Minister says that this is one means of impressing upon the people of Canada the fact that they must bear taxation. I do not think it is at all necessary to do that, because that fact has been impressed upon the people in more ways than one. As to its bringing in revenue and the statement that the people should be glad to contribute something to assist those who are destitute, and all that sort of thing, I cannot quarrel with that although I think every person in Canada who has the means is prepared to help those who might be less fortunate. However, this tax is in the form of a nuisance to the person who has to lick a stamp to place it upon a cheque, and to my mind the same revenue might have been raised in some other way which would have been less of a nuisance.

If this tax represented by the stamp is a recognition of a service b5f the community, wh}' should it not be proportionate to the amount of the cheque? If* one cheque is for $10 and another for $10,000, it seems to me that we might very well have
a proportionate amount collected since there would be a .larger service rendered by the community.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member is a
student of economics. He finds more time to read than I do, and he should realize that this matter was the subject of debate in the British House of Commons and House of Lords. The proportion of service rendered is not determined by the amount appearing on the face of the cheque; it matters not whether the cheque is for $10 or $10,000, the service rendered by the state is the same in both instances. It will be recalled that some years ago we had a tax based upon the amount of the cheque, but that was abandoned as being in every real sense a nuisance tax. There was the difficulty of making the correct computation, and I have seen promissory notes covered with stamps because of the small denomination available. There are many services rendered by the state which cannot be measured by the amount of income of the individual, by the amount of a particular commodity which he consumes or produces, or by the amount of wealth which he puts into circulation. In this instance it is perfectly clear that a $10 or a $10,000 cheque imposes upon the country the same obligation with respect to the preservation of law and order, freedom from attack, movement through the post, the law of merchants, and other services which provide for freedom of exchange and freedom of movement.

Those services are paid
for in proportion to the value which is rendered.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

A man pays assessment
according to the amount of property he owns, and his income tax is based upon the same principle.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The prosecution of
offenders, which is a provincial obligation, is not measured by the amount involved.
A man pays according to his property.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The measure of service
rendered is as great with respect to $10,000 as it is with respect to $10.
A man pays in proportion to the amount of property which is protected.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member asked
me why a cheque for $10,000 carried only the two cent tax imposed on a cheque for $10.
Special War Revenue Act

and he said that the amount of the tax should be measured by the amount of service rendered by the state. I pointed out that the state renders the same service with respect t-o the $10 cheque as it does with respect to the $10,000 cheque.

I would like
to disabuse the right hon. gentleman's mind of the apparent false impression he entertains of the anxiety of the people of this country to pay sales tax.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess

May I say a word with regard to the stamp tax as applied to creamery Cheques? The Prime Minister is aware that most of the agriculturists in this country today are selling their products below the cost of production. I have never yet sold any commodity that I have produced on my farm, and for which I have been paid by cheque, without having to pay the stamp tax on the cheque myself, no matter at what rate the stamp tax was. If I sell a carload of wheat and take payment by cheque, the stamps that are put on the cheque are charged to my account. On the other hand, if I issue a cheque for anything I buy I am compelled to put the stamp on the cheque. I would ask the Prime Minister if some way could not be found whereby the man who issues the cheque would put the stamp on himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the law now.

It may be the law, but when I go to the grain exchange and sell a carload of wheat at, say, $1,000, the full amount of the stamps put on the cheque is rharged to me on the bill, and previous to some years , ago the stamp tax was heavier than two cents. If I ship a can of cream to any dealer in Winnipeg the stamp tax on the cheque in payment will be charged to me no matter at what price I sell the cream. In the remarks that I made on the budget I cited the case of a friend of mine who shipped a can of cream to Winnipeg. I grant that it was not No. 1 cream, but he got $1.13 for it. Now under the present practice and the practice which has obtained ever since the stamp tax was imposed, the stamp put on the cheque in payment will be charged to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You can refuse a cheque and insist on cash.

I have taken the matter up with the firms myself and they say that

they have no means of absorbing that tax. The facts are just as I have stated to the Prime Minister. On any cheque that I have received in payment for any of the commodities I produce I have had to pay the tax, and on any cheques that I have issued in payment for goods I have had to pay the tax. I do not know if they are violating the law in not putting the stamps on the cheque. I would ask the Prime Minister if there is any way in which they can be prevented from doing that.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They are violating the law if they do not put the stamp on the cheque.

I am looking for a suggestion, not offering a criticism. I have had a good deal of complaint about it, and if there is any way in which the Minister of Finance can prevent the practice as it has been carried on in the past I would appreciate such action, and I am sure the people of this country would.
What amount of revenue does the Minister of Finance expect to obtain by the imposition of the stamp tax on cheques up to $10?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I stated this afternoon that the officials were not in a position to indicate clearly what they did expect.
I wonder if the Prime Minister would reply to the suggestion I made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has, for some reason, been imposed upon.
But all farmers are in the same position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The law prevents that action being taken and compels the issuer of the cheque to pay the stamp tax, and for this reason: The hon. gentleman under the circumstances he indicated was entitled to cash. If he takes a cheque instead of cash, it must be a cheque issued in compliance with the law, which means that they must issue a cheque upon which the stamp has been affixed. If there is any general violation of the provisions of the law in that regard, when the bill is in committee or on third reading, a section can be added to provide a penalty for those who do not affix a stamp against the issue of a cheque. But I think that that provision is there now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: One and a half per cent I think is the figure now.

We will say one and a half per cent. The banks no doubt have some other incidental expenses in the issuance of circulation. Now they lend that money to the general public of Canada at six and seven, and my friends from the west say even as high as eight per cent. That is discharging a very necessary function, no doubt, and I have no fault to find with giving the banks the right to lend that money, but I do submit that the amount of tax which they pay is not commensurate with the great privilege which is given to them by the Dominion of Canada. My suggestion briefly is this, that the Minister of Finance should replace this nuisance tax by making the circulation tax one or two or three per cent higher than it is to-day. That change would be made on the principle that was laid down here at least by myself, that the tax should be based on some service rendered by the state. I submit that a great service is rendered by the state when they allow the chartered banks to issue currency to the extent I have indicated. I submit my suggestion to the earnest consideration of the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry to say that the argument of my hon. friend is specious. I thought exactly as he thinks now in the statement he has just made to this house, until I investigated the facts. It is not correct to assume that the banks issue money by way of circulation to an amount equal to their capital, and then loan it at five or six or seven per cent.
They have that power.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They have the power so to do, but in practice they cannot do it.

Not to the full amount.
Mr, BENNETT:	Nor to anything like it.
The average return from the circulation, as indicated by the chartered banks of the Dominion, taking one year with another, leaves a very insignificant profit so far as I have been able to ascertain. If the hon. gentleman will take the trouble to look at the bank returns he will find a reason for this. In the first place we will take the example of bank "A" with a capital of $30,000,000 It has the right to issue circulation to the amount of another $30,000,000. The tax to the country is based on the average circulation, and I think at the moment the tax amounts to one and one-half per cent per annum, a very substantial sum of money. If however he will take the bank return for any given period of time he will find not only that the entire capital of the bank plus its average circulation for the month is locked up in specie and in bank premises, but that there usually is a balance the other way. That balance is made up by the bank's reserves against which i't may not issue circulation, except under exceptional circumstances during certain seasons. I am certain that any of the banks will be very glad to indicate clearly their dealings in respect of their circulation from year to year. I am disclosing no secret when I say to my hon. friend that I believed that was a very proper source to tax at a higher rate, and some years ago as well as recently I looked into the matter. On computations, which have been checked and are not challenged, it is found that the circulation is not a fund that may be loaned at 5, 6 or 7 per cent and from which may be deducted only the cost of management plus a tax of one and one-half per cent. The circulation being constantly in movement, and the bank being compelled 'to carry in its vaults unused packages of bills against situations which frequently arise; and the cost of printing being very large, as perhaps my hon. friend has learned-
No, not with us.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is found that the net profit arising from circulation is a very insignificant sum, and does not contribute
Special War Revenue Act

markedly to the bank's profits. At the present time the circulation fund is taxed ratably higher, considering the benefits which accrue to those who issue it, than most other items in our taxing system.

I should like to ask the
right hon. gentleman whether his investigations were made during the business of the past year, which we know has not been as good. There seem to be large sums of capital in the bank's vaults that in two years are loaned out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My investigations were
first made years ago because I entertained very strongly the view my hon. friend has just expressed. The figures as presented were verified, and as I have said the average from year to year indicated that the statements were correct. I have not any papers before me, because I had not anticipated the question which has now been brought to my attention, but the reports made by the heads of the institution, men who have gone into this matter in great detail, indicated that there was no foundation for the information which I held. May I say that my view at that time was exactly similar to that which my hon. friend has now expressed. I did not refer to last year's figures.
Mr. WOODSWOiRTH: Before the committee rose at six o'clock I had asked the Prime Minister why there should be a flat rate on cheques. I do not like the stamp tax at all, but it seems to me that if we are to have a stamp tax of the kind proposed such a tax ought to have some relation to the value of the cheque issued. The Prime Minister took the ground that the stamp tax really represents the maintenance of law and order, and that kind of thing, and that that was a service which was rendered equally to all in the community. I must disagree with that kind of reasoning. For some people law and order means the maintenance of a beautiful home with every comfort, travelling, the education of their families, and the like. For another man law and order means a struggle to the utmost degree to earn a precarious livelihood, that he must live on a mean street and must experience great difficulty in properly educating his family. To still another man law and order means that he must travel on freight trains in order to make a living at all, or in the hope of making one. I wonder at the Prime Minister taking the ground that the maintenance of law and order means the same thing to every citizen. It seems to me that since in practice there

is such a very great difference, the difference should be recognized in matters of taxation.
If I understand anything in connection with the principles of taxation I think it is a recognized principle that men should pay in accordance with their ability. I think the same principle should apply in this particular form of taxation. I cannot see why a man who issues a cheque for $10 should pay the same amount as a man who issues one for $10,000. That does not seem reasonable: certainly it is not in accordance with the generally accepted principles of just taxation.
Further than that the Prime Minister resorted to the argument that every citizen ought to be willing to do his bit, that he ought to play his part and that the very poorest ought to pay to the extent at least of two cents. That reasoning might be fair if it was not also urged that the millionaire ought to do his bit. I wish to suggest that the people across Canada are getting tired of being told that the poor man should pay what he can, and yet leam that the rich man claims special exemption and does not want to do anything more than the poorest man in the community. If we are to accept this form of taxation it seems to me only the barest justice that the taxation should bear some sort of relationship to the extent of the transaction as indicated by the amount of the cheque.

I wish to extend to the Minister of Finance a plea in connection with the two cent stamp on cheques and I may say that in doing so I am merely stating the representations of the people of my constituency.
Last Thursday at the town of Leduc I attended the United Farmers of Alberta convention in the constituency I have the honour to represent, and the matter of the two cent tax was one of the items with which the convention dealt. May I say to the Minister of Finance that the people in that constituency fully appreciate the necessity for securing revenue for the country. I think they also fully appreciate the fact that they have to pay their share, and I believe they are willing so to do. I think also that at least in imagination they have some idea of the difficulties which the Minister of Finance must face in trying fairly to tax all the people. We must realize that if one class secures an exemption to any extent other classes have an equal claim and no doubt will make such claims. If the Minister of Finance listens to all claims very soon he would have no revenue at all. The people dn my con-

Special War Revenue Act
stituency appreciate that fact. It is because we think that in connection with this particular tax a certain class of farmers are being discriminated against that I now extend to the Prime Minister this plea. If my remarks are not well founded, I shall not expect my right hon. friend to pay any attention; if they are, I should hope that he would at least give the matter some consideration.
It is the conviction of the small farmers who are shipping cream, butter and other dairy products two, three or four times a week that a two cent stamp on the small credit slips or cheques that they receive bears too high a proportion to their small incomes. Many of these cheques are for 30, 65, 70 and SO cents, SI, SI.50 and so forth, and by the end of the year they have paid a very considerable amount of their income in stamp tax-an amount which they think is much more than their fair share. Moreover, they argue that in addition to having to pay the stamp tax on these small cheques, they must also pay a two cent stamp on every cheque they draw. They do not object to this latter tax, but they are perturbed at having to pay two cents on their small cream cheques.
I know it is contended that the farmer does not pay the tax, that the dealer does. In this connection I think we must listen to the farmer himself, because surely he is the best judge as to whether he does or does not pay the tax. Mixed farming is extensively carried on in my constituency, and at this convention which I attended recently composed of delegates from all over the constituency, nearly every one of whom was shipping cream, they all maintained that they themselves paid the tax on their cream cheques. Let us assume, for instance, that the creamery or the dealer in cream and other dairy products has an annual overhead of about $150,000. The agent of the creamery or the proprietor of the business naturally is anxious to reduce that overhead or absorb it, and the question arises, can that be done more easily by increasing, the cost to the consumer, or by decreasing the price paid to the [DOT]farmer. Each finds that it is easier to ab-sord his overhead by taking the latter course; and so the farmer pays the stamp tax. But suppose the minister refuses to believe that that is so, then I refer him to the cooperative creameries. In this case the tax of course would come from the members themselves on every can of cream that they ship to the cooperative creameries. There can be no doubt that the farmer pays this tax.
The convention to which I have already referred urges the finance minister to make an exemption on cream cheques for amounts up to $5. That would relieve the smaller farmer. The farmer who is in a position to allow his cream credits to accumulate for two or three months can obtain his income at the price of a two cent stamp; but the poorer the farmer is the more necessary he finds it to take his small cheque ever}' time he ships a can of cream, and therefore he must pay the two cent tax on every cheque.
Now I ask the Minister of Finance to give consideration to this plea. I repeat, if the statements I have made cannot be substantiated I shall not expect the minister to pay any attention to my plea, but if he finds those statements are true, if he finds that the farmers do pay more than their share of the stamp tax since they get their income in these small cheques, then I ask him to make the exemption on all these small cheques up to S5.

I should like to say a word, Mr. Chairman, in confirmation of my hon. friend's statement. The committee will remember that some years ago the same condition prevailed when the tax was placed upon these smaller cheques, including the creamery cheques. A campaign of protest was carried on for some months, at the conclusion of which we managed to persuade the government then in power that our suggestion was the correct one, and that a tax on such small cheques was not fair to the farmer. But if the tax was not fair then, it is still less fair to-day, because of the low price of cream. Moreover, the small dairy farmer is further penalized by his very laudable attempt to ship the very best quality of cream and so get the best possible grading, because in order to do that he must ship his cream in small quantities and very frequently. The committee will realize that on thousands of cheques of 50, 70 and 75 cents a two cent stamp, small as it may seem, in the aggregate amounts to a very heavy tax. In my riding we have established one of the largest cooperative creameries; it is the headquarters of the Central Alberta Dairy Pool Limited. And naturally when it was announced that this two cent stamp tax on small cheques would be reimposed I got a number of protests. First of all I received this very short wire:
Estimate handling ninety thousand cream settlements during year proposed postage and cheque adds three cents each settlement twenty-seven hundred dollars annually. Sales tax on supplies adds another four hundred dollar
Special War Revenue Act

burden total tax thirty-one hundred. Can you do anything get cream coupons exempt from cheque tax otherwise pool members have to pay this. Average cream cheque at present two dollars and fifty cents.
That is the average of the ninety thousand cream settlements. In the letter which folows the manager of the pool discusses who pays the tax and says:
It is idle talk to say that the issuer of the coupon pays the tax, as the money comes from the cream, and the tax just increases the spread between butter-fat prices, and butter prices.
Which is obvious to anyone who knows anything about dairy matters, and particularly in respect to cooperative creameries where the members naturally share all the profit and bear all the costs. While I am not very hopeful, for I realize the tremendous obligation resting on the Prime Minister at the present time to obtain all the revenue possible, still I do believe he is anxious to obtain that revenue as fairly as possible and not add to the burdens of a class which he himself acknowledges is very heavily burdened. The committee will realize on a moment's reflection that whether this stamp tax is paid directly or indirectly by the man who ships the cream, it simply increases the already too great spread between the price of his butter fat and the price of the butter. I add my plea to that made by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) and others that the minister reconsider the matter. The amount of revenue may not be very considerable, but the principle is an important one, and the irritation caused is very great indeed.

I also desire to say a
word on this tax. It is a matter on which perhaps more than on any other I have received representations from my constituents and from other electors in the city of Montreal. I am not surprised that quite a number of hon. members have risen already to plead with the Minister of Finance to reconsider this part of his budget. We are somewhat at a disadvantage in discussing the matter now, because the minister himself is not in a position to state the exact revenue he expects from this cheque tax, and we are also at a further disadvantage at this stage of the discussion because we have before us resolutions covering only part of the budget. I think it would be easier to show that the Minister of Finance could easily make up the money he would lose by dropping this part of his budget if he would alter other sections which are now before the committee. In the general discussion which took place on the budget one of my efforts was to show 
that while the Minister of Finance had not hesitated to impose taxation on the common and poor people in a general way, he had shown some generosity towards certain classes whom we think are more able to pay. I am quite sure that if the minister now pays some attention to the representations being made with regard to the stamp tax on cheques, when he comes to another part of his budget it will be easy for him to make up what he would lose by dropping this feature of his proposals.
During this discussion it has struck me that while hon. members agree that this tax is not desirable they are not quite in accord as to how they would shape it themselves. My good friend the hon. member for North Waterloo presented the argument that this is a nuisance tax, that it is indefensible and that he would gladly do away with it. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre argued that if the tax is to be maintained, rather than collect it on small cheques he would have a scale, as we had some years ago, increasing the tax as the amount of the cheque is increased. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin made a half way proposal, that the minimum be $5 instead of $10.
When the Minister of Finance introduced his budget he made a remark in connection with this tax which rather impressed me; he said it would not make much difference to certain large companies who had embossed cheques. The minister stated that very often these companies used these cheques for amounts below $10. I can tell the minister that I am not speaking for those companies at all, but I do know that in my own constituency and in the city of Montreal at large there are a great many people who issue several cheques each month for less than $10 in order to pay the grocer, the butcher or perhaps the dry goods store. They will feel it very much if they have to add this amount, small though it may be, to every cheque they issue. There is also the other point, that special stamps must be used. That is a nuisance in itself; you have to look for the stamps and sometimes you have to go a considerable distance to secure them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is provided in the
act that postage stamps may be used.
Is that a new regulation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Then so much the better; I will withdraw that part of my argument. On the other hand, however, that will make it almost impossible to tell the revenue from

Special War Revenue Act
this particular tax, which will place us under an even greater handicap than is the case to-night. I share the views of the hon. member for North Waterloo, with certain reservations since this tax was introduced by the Liberal party some years ago. This is a nuisance tax, in that it is not defensible or justifiable on its principle. I do know that it has had the effect of influencing the poor and medium class people, for whom we usually speak, to do away with cheques to a certain extent, which shows that the imposition of even a small tax like this means something.
I repeat what I said a moment ago, that if the whole budget were before us I could at once put my finger on some of the provisions under which it would be easy to find many times the amount expected from this tax, but if the Minister of Finance feels that he must maintain the tax I would support the argument of my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre and say I would rather see the old scale restored than have the tax collected on these small cheques. I know the Minister of Finance is a man of decision; when he brings down something he does so with considerable vigour, but at the same time he is a practical business main and is quite willing to alter his views when he thinks he has good reason to do so. Yesterday he brought down a lengthy list of exemptions under the sales tax, and I think thereby improved his budget very considerably. I am quite sure that if he gives further consideration to the representations made this afternoon and to-night with regard to the tax on cheques, perhaps when the bill is before the house some amendments may be moved whereby the tax will start with cheques of $10. If he needs more money from that tax, he might increase the tax on the larger cheques, but I would strongly urge that he leave the small cheques exempted from any tax.

When the
two cent tax on cheques up to $10 was abolished by the Liberal government, that action was taken largely because of the agitation which arose throughout the country with regard to cream cheques, and undoubtedly the same agitation will arise again. When one considers the way this tax works on small cheques it is seen to be a very drastic tax indeed. The Minister of Finance stated this afternoon that to pyramid the tax on larger amounts was a process rather difficult of administration, but that is no more so than with cheques for smaller amounts. I admit that this will produce a very large revenue. As one hon. gentleman stated just a few moments
ago, ordinary cream cheques are for $2 or $2.50. On an amount of $10 made up of those cheques there would be a very considerable contribution to the federal treasury, and our experience was that we would be much better off to forego what was termed, together with other taxes of a similar character, this nuisance tax and secure our revenue from some other source. I quite appreciate the necessity of raising revenue, but I think the government are drying up other prolific sources of revenue by the excessive application of tariffs. If these nuisance taxes are to be reestablished for the purpose of securing revenue because other sources are being lost, then we are likely to have a great crop of them. On the other hand, from an administrative standpoint I think the government would be well advised to consider leaving the two cent stamp tax on cheques for $10 or more, though even that is an unfair tax. My right hon. friend sought to defend it this afternoon, but after all it is easy of administration. After the change was made I did not hear that any considerable agitation arose against the imposition of the two cent tax on cheques of $10 or more, so I think the government would be well advised to consider dropping this resolution, as they have done with several others.

I can easily see that this two cent tax will be quite a burden, because I understand that it covers money orders, postal notes, pay cheques and travellers' cheques, most of which affect the farmer, the labourer and the poor man throughout the country. I can readily see that it would be adding to the already heavy burden which they have to bear. The Prime Minister this afternoon said something to the effect that the tax would be a sort of patriotic contribution towards the maintenance of the country's institutions in this present emergency. I admit that. There is not a Canadian who would not be glad to help Canada at this time. It seems to me, however, that people might express their patriotism in proportion to their ability to pay. Suppose we decided upon 2 cents up to $100, exempting cheques up to $10; then for the next $100 the tax would be 4 cents. And so on up to a certain limit. That would be a true test of patriotism, and the man who could issue a cheque for $200 would feel glad to contribute 4 cents; while the smaller business men would contribute according to their means. I think of the many expenditures which the farmer has to make: he has to keep up his insurance premium; he has to send money orders to the business houses in the cities, and he has to spend money in various
Special War Revenue Act

other ways. In my opinion it will be not only difficult to collect this tax, but it will be also an injustice to impose an additional burden upon the farmer when he is already overburdened. And this applies not only to farmers but to thousands of poor people throughout the country.
I should like to get some information from the Prime Minister in regard to drainage tiles for agricultural purposes, which I see are exempt. Are we to interpret "agricultural purposes" here to include drainage tiles for roadsides in the construction of municipal roads? Thousands of tiles are used for that purpose..

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Used by whom?

I presume, by the municipal council. It is further provided that crushed stone produced or manufactured by any municipality exclusively for use in building or maintaining roads or sidewalks, and not for sale, and sand, gravel and rubble, shall pay the tax. There are many privately-owned gravel and sand pits, the owners of which will have to pay the sales tax. I wonder how that will be collected.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am told that there is no change now in this item. With respect to tiles used for agricultural purposes, for drainage on the farm, out to the drain, there has been no tax. On tiles used by the municipal council there has been a tax. As regards gravel, crushed stone and rubble, the. tax has been collected from the proprietor who sold it and not from the municipality that used it in connection with the maintenance of highway facilities within the boundary of the municipality. I remember on one occasion

not in parliament-urging upon the minister of that day some such provision, the matter having been brought to my attention on the train; and that government later provided that no collection should be made when the gravel or crushed stone is used for the purposes of the municipality.
I am under the impression that there has been a decision of the department to the effect that stone, rubble and gravel are not taxable even when taken from the individual pit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am told that when it is sold by the proprietor the tax has been exacted. It may be that in the particular instance to wffiich the hon. gentleman has referred the tax collector might not have been sufficiently well informed to collect the tax.
This was a decision of the department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am told by the commissioner that it is taxable. With respect to the tax on cheques, it was- to remove the nuisance feature that the tax was made of universal application. The nuisance arose from the fact that in one instance a cheque for $12 had to have a stamp, while a cheque for $9 had not. With the use of embossed cheques, provided free by the banks, except for the charge for embossing, the result in many instances was that a cheque for an amount under $10 was written on that form of cheque, and it was a nuisance for one to remember that a cheque under $10 did not need the stamp.
People are no better off this way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In this instance all
cheques carry the stamp, and there is no necessity for remembering that the tax is not payable on cheques under a given amount. There is one hon. member in this house who likes to suggest that one is always thinking in terms of companies. I am not thinking of companies at all. One of my colleagues told me that, in paying for household goods, his wife always used the embossed cheque, and she sometimes discovered that she need not have used a cheque providing for the 2 cent tax. One does not use a different cheque book in writing cheques for amounts under $10. With regard to the representations made to reduce the amount to $5, for the reason that some cream cheques are less than $1, I shall take the matter into careful consideration before the bill is disposed of. The government will consider these representations and determine whether or not such action as suggested is warranted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do I understand that in regard to the postage stamp there is an addition of one cent excise which is applicable only to letters within Canada, and not to letters addressed to other parts of the empire?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
All letters originating in Canada, wherever destined, pay the one cent tax. Already the drop letter, so-called, pays the one cent. That is to say, the local rate in Ottawa is two cents, one cent postage and one cent tax. When the government of my right hon. friend removed the one cent tax from three cent letters they did not remove it from the drop letters in the cities. The result was that the rate was one cent plus one cent tax. There has now been added to all other letters an additional one cent. My hon. friend from Gloucester last evening asked a question with respect to the air mail service. He will find

Special War Revenue Act
that the section does cover the air mail, because it refers to all mail which is handled by post, and the one cent applies to all letters and postal cards that are transported by post, which has a definite meaning under our institutions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The section
provides that there shall be levied and collected on every letter for transmission by post, over any distance within Canada, a tax of one cent in addition to postage payable. That is only for letters posted in Canada. The postage has been two cents anywhere within Canada, and penny postage throughout the empire. As I read the section, there will hereafter be penny postage throughout the empire, but letters carried over any distance within Canada will have to pay the additional one cent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is only a way of expressing it. Every letter that moves any distance in Canada will pay an additional cent. A letter cannot reach any part of the empire without travelling through Canada, and it also pays the one cent. The language used in the section is only a form of expression, but all letters originating in Canada will pay the additional cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In other words, it is three cents within Canada and throughout the empire?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Is the one per cent special excise tax imposed on duty free goods?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My first impression seems to have been correct. Duty free value, as defined iby the statute, means free goods, and the value is their fair market value. That is defined by statute.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hereafter there is to be a tax on everything that comes into Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, one per cent. With respect to the point raised by my hon. friend from Quebec South, I may say that the decision of the department was made on August IS, 1928, that crushed stone produced or manufactured by any municipality exclusively for maintaining roads and not for sale shall be free, and not otherwise. That was made by order in council following the recommendation of the department, on August 18, 1928.

That means that thousands of farmers throughout the country who have small pits will have to keep track of what
they sell hereafter that does not go to road construction. And the tile makers throughout the Dominion will have to differentiate between tiles sold for agricultural purposes and the few odd tiles they sell for other purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no change in the law - as it has been administered since 1928. It may be that the fanner very seldom makes a claim. He may be very frequently asked to make it. But I am referring to what the law is and has been, and I have stated what it is and has been since August 18, 1928.
That may be all right, but still I think the thing is going to be a nuisance and a very hard matter to enforce.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Has it been?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The commissioner tells me that there has not been any trouble.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In view of what my right hon. friend has just said about this one cent tax applying to everything, I asked him a little earlier if he would indicate whether or not an exception would be made in the case of small articles brought into the country as the result of purchase in the course of a visit to the adjoining country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have noted that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As the resolution now stands, unless those articles are brought in by mail or express, in which case they are exempt up to $25, they will be taxed. Under the proposed law if one takes a trip to the United States and purchases $5 worth of goods, he would have to declare those goods and pay the tax.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have made a notation upon the margin of my bill to look into that matter.

I appreciate the assurance of the Prime Minister that the representations made with regard to fixing a minimum of $5 in the case of the cheque tax will receive consideration, and we hope that that may be a forecast of favourable action. I submit that there can be no logical reason for not having that same exemption apply to money orders, travellers' cheques and receipts for money.
