speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In my judgment, the application would be to all.

My right hon. friend has said that in connection with the handling of money the tax is a small fraction of the amount involved, but two cents on a $10
Special War Revenue Act
Is there to be a two cent charge on every money order?
Certainly.

Would the Minister of
Finance look into the effects of that tax upon the revenue of the Post Office Department? Take a post office order for one dollar, there would be a two cent stamp on that, plus the tax, which would make it four cents.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There would be a two cent stamp on it if it were being sent away; two cents for the letter, and two cents for the money order.

The cost of the money order would be two cents, and then there would be the two cent stamp on it, making a total of four cents for a small order, and then one cent extra postage. The people would be apt to use cheques and discontinue the buying of money orders. The committee is aware that the mail order business is earned on mostly by post affice orders, and to my mind this would be a direct tax upon the ladies of the household who do most of the buying from these mail order houses. It would entail three cents additional expense in the case of each small purchase. The leader of the opposition referred to parties return-

ing from a trip to some other country and bringing in certain articles. I have a case before the customs department in connection with a person' who spent the winter in England. A fur coat was purchased in that country but upon arrival in Montreal in May or June the coat was held by the customs department until the duty of $36 had been paid. This seemed to me to be rather an extreme case, as the coat had been worn all through the winter months. It seems the customs officials have the right to do that. Now I suppose the excise tax and the sales tax will be added to that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That has nothing to do
with either the sales tax or the excise tax on the statement as made. I know nothing about the case, but just listening to the statement of the hon. gentleman I would say it was a seizure because of failure to make a declaration.

The department ruled
that it was quite within the jurisdiction of the customs officials to tax articles brought in in that way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There always has been
the right on the part of the customs authorities to make a seizure where there has been no declaration, and if the customs officials had not been told of the coat which the hon. gentleman referred to it would be competent for them to seize it. I understand that that has always been the law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
To come back to the additional one cent tax on postage in Canada. I wish to see if I understand exactly what my right hon. friend means. Is there any necessity whatever for the words " for any distance within Canada." The resolution reads:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend section seventy-one of the Special War Revenue Act, chapter one hundred and seventy-nine of the revised statutes, and to provide that there shall be levied and collected on every letter for transmission by post for any distance within Canada a tax of one cent, in addition to postage payable.
I would interpret that as having been intended originally to mean that the additional one cent postage applied to letters that were mailed in Canada and were to go any distance within Canada but would not include letters to go beyond Canada. I may be mistaken in that. The Prime Minister is quite sure. I would ask if there is any necessity to retain those words " for any distance within Canada " in order to give the meaning he is now placing upon it?

Special War Revenue Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I can only say to my
right hon. friend that the draftsmen have used this language as covering the end sought to be attained. That is, if it was transmitted by post for any distance within Canada it paid the additional tax. To be truthful, when I read it, I assumed that they had in mind the possibility of letters posted on outgoing ships and matters of that kind. I do not know whether that was meant by it or not, but clear it is that this covers it in any event.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I imagine it is just a case where the draftsman has become a little confused [between my right hon. friend's policy of Canada first and his policy of Empire first. He evidently thought at the outset that the intention was to be Empire first, and then came to the conclusion that it had better be Canada first, and between the two he did not know just what to do, and so he left the whole paragraph ambiguous.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman spoke just a little too soon, for we have adopted exactly the language of his statute, and have merely added the words, " letter and ". So whatever conflict there might be between Canada first and Empire first, we find ourselves in accord in this instance.

That clause applied because we had a two cent rate all over the empire Now you are having a three cent rate. Does that apply to the empire as a whole, or to the British possessions, the Union of South Africa, and so forth?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. We have merely added the words, " letter and
For any distance within Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The exact words that were there before. If it moves any distance in Canada it pays the one cent before it goes out of Canada, whether it goes to the United States or to another part of the empire or anywhere else.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My right hon. friend says that I spoke a little too soon. I may say to him that perhaps he ha3 spoken a little too soon. In order to interpret his own act I observe that he has had to go back to our legislation, as he has done in most matters of this kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is pleasing in turn to realize that my right hon. friend's legislation was copied or taken from his predecessor's.

If I might revert for a moment to the question that was asked some time ago by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Cayley) and referred to by the hon. member for Quebec South, that is, the matter of sales tax on stone and gravel if produced by the individual farmer, my impression was very strong that we had exempted the small individual farmer who sold an occasional load of sand or gravel from the operation of the sales tax because it was almost impossible to collect if. It was my impression, and I have verified it, that an order in council was passed exempting the small farmer from the payment of that tax.

Exempting everybody, and it 'is in the resolution itself. If the Prim? Minister will read it I think he will come to the conclusion that the resolution itself specifies that sand, gravel, rubble and field stone are exempt. I do not think it is worth while having any discussion about it, but if the Prime Minister will read the resolution he will find that the order in council to which he referred a moment ago says that crushed stone produced by a muncipality is free and sand, gravel, rubble and field stone no matter by whom produced are free. I am quite sure that that is the interpretation given by the department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is the other way.
I yield to my right hon. friend's superior legal knowledge.

As I understand, it, you are permitted to put either an excise stamp or a postage stamp on cheques. How are you going to differentiate between the two departments as to revenue? Where are you going to give credit? You cannot give credit for the whole to the National Revenue department, for they can only get credit for the excise stamps issued by them and the returns made. The Post Office Department would have to get credit for the postage stamps used on cheques. That will not give you as much revenue as though you used excise stamps altogether because under the Postal Act you have to pay 70 cents up to five thousand, and 50 cents between five and ten thousand, so you have a 50 per cent and 70 per cent deduction from the revenue you anticipate on that transaction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no doubt about what the hon. gentleman says. This is done to accommodate the people and remove what might be considered a nuisance. The Post Office Department will get credit for all postage stamps sold during the year, and the
Special War Revenue Act

National Revenue department for the others. It is amazing the complaints made by people that they cannot conveniently use a two cent stamp, which most people have in a pocket book or elsewhere on their person.

Do away with the excise
stamp and leave it to the post office entirely.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have always had some
doubt as to how it came into being, but it did, and we are merely providing that either may be used.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
May I say
a word as to how it came into being? One is not expected to disclose anything that takes place in the cabinet but controversy was carried on in this house so perhaps I may speak of what occurred here. That I remember very well, there being considerable discussion on the point as to whether it was advisable to keep the revenues of the two departments separate and distinct, and Mr. Bureau, who was then Minister of Inland Revenue, made out a very strong case before his colleagues and this house on the advisability of issuing separate and distinct stamps for revenue purposes. I quite well recall that at that time it was thought in the public interest to keep the two separate although it would involve the inconvenience which my right hon. friend has spoken of. I believe it would be well for him to discuss the matter very thoroughly, with both the Postmaster General and the Minister of National Revenue, if he has not already done so, before making a decision.

I remember distinctly that this discussion came up some years ago when the Hon. Mr. Bureau was Minister of National Revenue. Up to a certain time one either could use postage stamps or excise stamps on cheques. It was shown that the government was not receiving a great deal of revenue, due to the fact that if postage stamps were bought the postmaster received the most of the revenue and, of course he kept it. Although I cannot remember the exact year, a change was made in the law to the effect that only excise stamps would be used, and in that way the government received a great deal more revenue. It seems to me there is no reason why that should not be carried out in this instance. Wherever stamps are required for cheques I think the postmasters in the little country districts or towns should be supplied with excise stamps to sell to their people so that the government might receive the whole of the revenue.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is what is done now.

I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister upon the change providing that the public may use either postage or excise stamps. I should be pleased to see excise stamps eliminated altogether. I do not think anything has caused more inconvenience in connection with the stamp tax than has the necessity for keeping both kinds of stamps on hand. The convenience o-f the public will be well served by the change which is being made.
May I ask the. minister if there is any considerable volume of business in connection with fire insurance, particularly by foreign companies, on which he has imposed the 15 per cent?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It will be observed by those who have read the section dealing with the 15 per cent tax that it does not come into effect until a proclamation has been made. There are in this country a very large number of fire insurance agents extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific who receive 15 per cent of the premiums on the services they render. They have felt that owing to the necessity of their maintaining offices in Canada they should not be subjected to the competition I have mentioned. That competition at the moment pays a 5 per cent tax. As I have said this tax is now under litigation and it is expected the privy council will deal with the matter this summer. Litigation is pending in which the validity of the tax is questioned
I do not just follow the remarks of my right hon. friend. Does he refer to a tax on foreign companies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes; that is now under litigation. This increase from 5 per cent to 15 per cent will not result in the greater amount being collected until a proclamation is made bringing it into force. I am informed that a number of the provinces have made a rather heavy impost on similar companies, and all that will be carefully considered before a proclamation is made. I have mentioned that, although I could go into more detail if required. I think however the hon. gentleman realizes that the. rate bears some relation to the rate which our people have been receiving for the issuance of policies and the collection of premiums in connection with their own Canadian business. The proclamation bringing this measure into effect will not be made without the fullest information.
Would it be possible to make a levy of less than 15 per cent?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is a levy of 5 per cent being made now, and that will continue until the proclamation.

Special War Revenue Act
If it were decided that 15 per cent were too much, could it not be made 10 per cent?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not as it stands in this statute.
My right hon. friend would not have discretion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That discretion is not granted. However the hon. gentleman has made a suggestion which I may frankly say I had not considered. It is worthy of consideration. I think my hon. friend is referring to a percentage not less than 5 and not more than 15.
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not usual, but I shall consider the suggestion because. I think it is worthy of consideration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not wish to take up the time of the committee in discussing further the matter of postage. I do believe, however, the question is more involved than would appear on the surface. The Post Office Department differs from some other departments of the public service in that it is a public service department. The payment for postage is a payment for services rendered by the state as distinct from payment of a tax for revenue purposes. If my right hon. friend's present intentions are carried out I am afraid he will find that if there is any considerable amount of revenue raised from the tax the Post Office Department will soon reach the position where there will be surpluses rather than deficits, and pressure will be brought to bear upon my right hon. friend to reduce postage. In so doing, however, he will really deprive himself of a source of revenue which would have remained to him if he had kept the revenue of the Department of National Revenue entirely separate and distinct from that of the Post Office Department. I know that at the time the former administration decided to insist upon the use of revenue stamps on cheques my feeling was exactly as that of my right hon. friend at the present time. I felt that to make the public buy revenue stamps would impose an additional obligation, and that as most everyone would have postage stamps in his pocket it would be infinitely more convenient to use postage stamps on cheques. After having gone into the matter, however, and having listened to a full discussion between the Minister of National Revenue and the Postmaster General, all the members of the former administration were convinced that it was highly 22110-208
desirable to keep the two sources of revenue entirely separate and distinct, to keep the post office revenue in its own account and the revenue of the Department of National Revenue in another. I think the matter is worthy of careful consideration.

In support of what has
been said by the leader of the opposition let me draw the attention of the right hon. gentleman to two facts which have occurred to my mind. There were over eight and a half million postal notes issued last year. Taking those postal notes at one cent each we have a revenue of about $80,000 or $85,000. There were about seventeen million money orders issued, bringing in a revenue of about $350,000 at the 2 cent rate. Those postal notes and post office money orders will all bear the two cent postage stamp, because they are sold in the post office, and revenue stamps will not be placed on them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think they always have, have they not?

No, there have been no
postage stamps used on cheques in the last three or four years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, not on chequeson postal notes.

Yes, exactly. Lately, however, there has been no excise revenue stamp in the shape of a 2 cent postage stamp on post office orders. There has been a regular fee charged by the post office which was figured in ratio to the amount of the order. Apart from that, however, we have one cent in the case of postal notes and two cents for money orders. Instead of that money going to excise, at least $430,000 of it will go to the Post Office Department.
As an ex-Postmaster General I wish to see the Post Office Department get all the revenue possible, and while this $400,000 odd will give an increase to the rural postmasters at the rate of 50 per cent in one case and 70 per cent in the other, thereby increasing their remunerations, and while I am perfectly satisfied to see that take place, yet if that action is being taken for revenue purposes to swell the receipts of the excise department I think my hon. friend is missing the mark, because he will not get that revenue for the excise department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no doubt that
the ex-Postmaster General is correct in his statement. However, the moneys go to the same pool in the end, namely, the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.

Special War Revenue Act

I beg your pardon, not in the rural districts. There are at least four thousand post offices, the revenue of which does not go into the consolidated revenue fund; it is paid to these postmasters under commission.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Of course, but the surplus goes into the revenues of the country. My hon. friend does not mean for a moment that any surplus does not reach the consolidated revenue fund?
No, it does not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Excuse me. Once every month an adjustment is made. The rural postmasters cannot put the money into their pockets; it goes into the revenues of the country the same as the excise tax. The postmasters have been selling excise stamps during the last two years.
No sir, they have not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They did, but they are not now. I stand corrected in relation to that. But it is a question of balancing the convenience against the inconvenience; that is all it is. What the hon. gentleman has said has been considered, I think, by every member of the government, as to whether or not this provision is one which should find its place in the statutes. It is a question whether or not a man who usually has on his person a two cent postage stamp in his pocket book, and should find himself unable to write a cheque without violating the law because he has no excise stamp and cannot get one, should be able to use his postage stamp and issue the cheque. If not, he is violating the law by issuing his cheque without placing a stamp upon it, and is incurring a possible penalty of $50. I have no very fixed conviction about it, but my view was, weighing the balance of convenience and inconvenience, that it was a convenient thing to use a postage stamp. In view of what has been said by the right hon. gentleman and by the former Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) I will have the matter again investigated by the officials with whom I have already discussed it. If there is any insuperable reason why the proposal should not be adopted, we will not proceed further with it; but if it does appear that it would be a convenience to all those who issue cheques, I think the balance of convenience should be respected. If I thought by retaining this proposal we should be able to balance the income and outgo of the postal department next year, I think the right hon. gentleman would agree with me that it would be a splendid experiment to keep it there. But I do not think he need

have any fear because the postal department is not making a profit to-day that we can balance the account merely by exchanging postage stamps for excise stamps in the manner indicated.
There is another point to be considered-after to-day we shall be using the three cent postage stamp and the two cent stamp will be a rarity.
You can attach two ones.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I entirely agree with the Prime Minister as to the question of convenience, but sooner or later the question of revenue is going to come up in connection with both the Post Office Department and the Department of National Revenue. It is dangerous to prophesy, but I do venture to predict that if the matter is left as my right hon. friend now proposes he will find that his revenues will drop very perceptibly in the Department of National Revenue and those of the Post Office Department will increase to the point where there is a surplus. Then great pressure will be brought to bear upon him to bring back postage to a two cent basis-pressure that he will not be able to resist if times improve, as we all hope they will. The public generally will become confused as to the reason for the improved position of the postal revenue, and we will find it difficult to explain how the post office revenues have increased while others have fallen off.

I do not want to delay
this item, but let me point out again to the Prime Minister that the additional two cents on money orders and the additional cent on postal notes, with the additional cent on air mail service will bring him an additional revenue of $800,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is splendid.
That is what you are going to get.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You are going to lose it from the Department of National Revenue.

But of that you are going
to lose $400,000 from the national revenue department. I think if the right hon. gentleman will look into these figures he will find that I am correct within $50,000 I base my calculations from my knowledge of the department on the quantity of mail carried last year by the air service. From the two cent routes you will get an extra $199,000; from the five cent routes $80,000 to $85,000; and from your postal notes and money orders the revenue will be over $420,000. I am with the right

Special War Revenue Act
hon. gentleman on the question of convenience, but I want him to know what revenue he is receiving for the taxes that are being imposed. He will not know it from the postal department, and consequently the people will have no knowledge of the amount of taxation which has been imposed upon them in this way.

Mr. Chairman, I think it
is highly desirable that the government should know exactly what revenue is obtained from this particular source. I think it is just as desirable that the public be inconvenienced as little as possible. On which side the balance turns I am not prepared to say, but possibly both purposes could be served in this way. Would it not be possible, since all the cheques go through the various clearing houses in our cities, to have a record of the exact number of cheques that are handled throughout the year; multiply that number by two and you have your revenue in dollars and cents; then you can deduct that from your total receipts in the Post Office Department and you have the excise stamp revenue also.

The stamp duty is reimposed
on the small cheques in order to gain revenue. If people are allowed to use a postage stamp instead of an excise stamp on these cheques, for every dollar's worth of stamps which are so used the government will receive only 50 per cent, or perhaps 35 per cent in post office revenue. So there is not going to be very much revenue received by the government from this tax if they are to receive this small percentage. If the postmasters of the various districts are going to get 50 per cent commission, or whatever it may be, we might as well go back to the old system of not putting stamps on cheques of $10 and under. If it is not compulsory to use excise stamps on cheques I think you will find the government will get little, if any, revenue, from this source of taxation. With regard to the convenience or inconvenience of the public, I think I know something about the rural districts where the people .might be inconvenienced by not being allowed to place a postage stamp on cheques. To-day if I make out a cheque for payment of an account here, and I have no excise stamp in my pocket. I hand the payee two cents, and when he gets down to the bank he buys a excise stamp and places it on the cheque. That practice is followed all over Canada. If a man way back in the country makes payment by cheque, and has no excise stamp handy, all he has to do is to hand out two cents and when the cheque is deposited at the bank it is duly 22110-20Si
stamped. In this way the law is fulfilled in the spirit if not in the letter. Nine or ten years ago I had as much to do as anybody with convincing the finance minister of those days of the desirability of requiring excise stamps to be used on cheques. If the government expect any revenue from this source there is only one thing to do. It will not inconvenience the people to any great extent to put excise stamps on cheques, and the government will get practically all the revenue from those stamps, since the customs officers only receive a commission of one-half or one per cent. I strongly recommend to the government that they decide not to allow the postmasters to sell the stamps which will be placed on cheques, because as I said a moment ago there will be no revenue to the government. The postmasters in the different districts will have their salaries increased much more than is necessary. I remember during the war, when this tax was put on first, that several cases came to my notice where postmasters had doubled their salaries, and in the towns many postmasters received a great deal more revenue than they were entitled to receive, through the sale of these postage stamps for use on cheques and notes, especially when the tax was graduated. I know something about this matter; I live in and represent a rural constituency, and I say the government need have no fear of inconveniencing the people. I would lay down the law that excise stamps should be used only for the purpose of cheques or notes.

I must take issue with my
hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough. In practice it will work out that the person wishing to put a stamp on a cheque will find he has only a three cent stamp, because now it will cost three cents for a letter. The result will be that the government, in an indirect and I think wholly improper way, will get a greatly increased revenue. One cent stamps will not be in general circulation; every person will buy three cent stamps.

He can put on two
one cent stamps.

He could put on two one
cent stamps, but he is not likely to have them. I believe it is more than probable that in at least twenty-five per cent of the cases the cheques will bear a three cent stamp, and the government will derive that additional revenue.
No, the postmaster will get it.

The postmaster will get
perhaps fifty per cent, but the government
Special War Revenue Act

will be getting more than it should get. On the other hand, my hon. friend speaks of people in the rural districts and suggests that the postmasters be allowed to sell excise stamps. The postmasters will not do that unless they are paid a commission, and if you pay a commission it might as well be paid on postage stamps. One of the points stressed most strongly by persons who have discussed the budget with me has been, "Let us get away from the nuisance of having to carry excise stamps." I do believe that the vast majority of people who give out small cheques would much prefer to attach a postage stamp to them rather than an excise stamp.

If I might try to sum
up this discussion, I find that every hon. member is agreed on two points. In the first place, we all agree that it would be a great convenience to do away with the excise stamp and use a postage stamp instead. In the second place we are agreed that it is desirable to be able to tell what is the amount of revenue from the post office and what is the amount from other sources.
Perhaps it is possible to conciliate those two points. If we think it would be a great convenience for the public to have just the one stamp possibly we could get the information we desire in some way other than by selling different stamps. The hon. member for North Waterloo made a suggestion a moment ago which appeals to me. The banks might be able to report the number of cheques that have gone through the clearing house, and in that way it would be very easy to find out the tax paid on cheques. The same thing could be done in the Post Office Department. My good friend the former Postmaster General, by merely looking at the estimates, has been able to tell us that this will involve about $400,000. If by a casual glance at the estimates the former Postmaster General, whose ability I admit to be above par, is able to say what this will mean, surely the Post Office Department under my genial friend will be able to establish the same thing. The Post Office Department knows how many postal notes are issued in a year. If there is a fixed amount of taxation, be it one cent or two cents on every postal note or other note issued by the post office, then it will be the duty of the Postmaster General in making his report to mention the amount paid by way of taxation on those notes. Therefore we will know, when the revenue of the Post Office Department is given to this house, that a certain percentage of that revenue really belongs to the Department of National Revenue.

I therefore submit, Mr. Chairman, that we should make every effort to retain in the bill the sections which permit the general public to use postage stamps, which I suppose will mean the eventual disappearance of the excise stamp, and greater care should be taken by the government to establish by Statistics the amount of taxation collected not only in connection with letters but from all other sources requiring the affixing of a stamp.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend the ex-Postmaster General entirely overlooked the fact that as the law now stands, under sections 69 and 70 of the Special War Revenue Act the stamp affixed to a money order is a two cent postage stamp. These are the words:
No money order for an amount exceeding ten dollars shall be issued under the provisions of the Post Office Act unless there is affixed thereto or to the relative advice a postage stamp of the value of two cents.
So as an actuarial computation the statement of the ex-Postmaster General does not seem to have much value, because under the statute as it was the two cent stamp had to be affixed.
Are you not now adding two cents more?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
Yes, you are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. Then the next section reads:
No postal note for an amount exceeding ten dollars shall be issued under the provisions of the Post Office Act until there is affixed thereto a postage stamp of the value of one cent, to be paid for by the purchaser of the note.
Those are additions to the cost of the note and the money order at the moment, and we are merely providing that i!t may be a postage or other stamp. There is no additional two cents.
But the additional revenue is to be derived by reason of the fact that you are now taxing a money order or postal note, a travellers' cheque or a bank cheque, the amount of which is below $10.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But that is not what the hon. gentleman said. He read from the report that 17,000,000 money orders and 8,900,000 postal notes had been issued, and he proceeded to make his computation as though they were all for amounts less than $10, but that number included all the notes and orders, whatever their value. As the statute now stands the tax is paid by postage stamp and not by excise stamp. As my hon. friend will observe, the revenues of the Post Office Department

Special War Revenue Act
were swollen by the two cents in the case of the money order and the one cent in the case of the postal note. The amendment merely makes it applicable to all money orders or postal notes whether over or under 110, and the computation made by the ex-Postmaster General, he will see at once, is as far beside the question as it is possible to be.
You are reading from the revised statutes of 1927?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Is there an excise or postage stamp affixed to-day to postal notes and money orders, for excise purposes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If they are over 110, for war revenue purposes; that is what I am told.
Shall I report the resolution?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is a part of the bill which has to do with exemptions from the operation of the Excise Act which heretofore having been granted, as well as others which have come before the department for consideration. One is the sale, transfer or assignment of bonds and debentures of the Dominion of Canada, about which some doubt existed The next is the assignment of the allotment ot the shares of any association, company or corporation; and the new one is the sale to any person resident and domiciled without Canada of any bond, debenture or share of debenture stock transferable by delivery to bearer.
That is new.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but I fancy it is not unfamiliar to members of the house. While it has not been observed in practice, it imposed a penalty upon Canadians as against foreign brokers when they made transfers.

The Prime Minister will remember that some days ago I had the pleasure of a conference with him with regard to the purely farm mutual companies engaged in fire and weather insurance. I asked whether he would consider putting them in the same category as the fraternal benefit societies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not in this resolution.
I thought that insurance came under this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, only the excise
feature.
The insurance question came up a short time ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That was another matter. If there is any doubt about it, I will discuss the matter when the bill is in committee. I understand it is in the other bill. I wish to protect my hon. friend, so that his position will not be prejudiced.

I wish to direct the attention of the Minister of Finance to the excise tax proper of one per cent, which is a brand new tax. My right hon. friend says it applies to present duty free goods as well as to dutiable goods. He has provided certain exemptions from that tax, not very many, but exemptions which I submit do require some explanation. I have in mind two. First there is an exemption from this one per cent tax of material used for the manufacture of binder twine for export. I should like to know why that exemption is restricted to material used in the manufacture of binder twine for export and not in the manufacture of binder twine for use in this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This tax as it stands applies to all articles, free or otherwise. The exemptions apply to raw leaf tobacco, and so on, and fish and other products of Newfoundland, and the material used in the manufacture of binder twine for export, there having grown up a considerable body of export business. If under the law as it stands that tax were imposed it might have the effect, because of the fiscal laws of other countries, of destroying that export trade. And that is something that has to be very carefully considered in relation to many of these articles. So far as I can see, this is the only one that stands in that position.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My right hon. friend will discover that international competition along many lines has become so keen that the imposition of a one per cent excise tax may mean the difference between our exporters losing altogether 'certain markets they have to-day and their being able to retain them. That is the 'great danger of this one per cent tax, and it is the objection which, of course, we have to the general imposition of customs duties foy my right hon. friend. I venture to say that what is going to happen as a result of the imposition of extended customs tariffs is that a large part of the export market will be lost altogether, and lost for the simple reason that competition has become so keen in the markets of the world that the placing of this extra burden upon
Special War Revenue Act

our own manufacturers and producers will make it impossible for them successfully to compete abroad.

Let me now refer to the next exemption. I do not think my right hon. friend has given any reason why the first exemption which I have mentioned should not apply to binder twine used in this country. It is all very well to give a benefit to the foreign market, but at the same time those who use binder twine in this country should have the benefit of exemption from this one per cent excise tax. I want to ipoint out also the exemption mentioned by my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guy^borough-the exemption of fish and other fish products of Newfoundland'. My right hon. friend gave as a reason for that exemption the fact that there was some convention with Newfoundland. I have looked up the act, and there is no convention. Perhaps my right hon. friend has something else in mind. There is no convention which prevents the imposition of an excise tax on that fish. The exemption contained in section 8 of the Customs Tariff Act is to the effect that, notwithstanding anything in that act, fish and all other products of the fisheries of Newfoundland may be imported into Canada free of customs duty until otherwise determined by the governor in council, by order published in the Canada Gazette. So that there is nothing about any convention. There is nothing to prevent my right hon. friend from imposing this unusual one per cent excise tax on that fish. But that is not the worst of it. The right hon. gentleman in his declaration, that he is going to impose an excise tax on articles which are free as well as on articles that are dutiable, is striking at the fishing industry in this country in two ways. In the first place he is letting in fish from Newfoundland exempt from the excise tax; and in the second place he is taxing what is now free, the rope used by the fishermen as one of their implements of production. The fishermen, therefore, are being struck from both sides by this one percent excise tax, and I ask my right hon. friend seriously to consider whether an implement of production such as rope, which is a raw material used by these men in carrying on their industry, should not 'be exempt in order to assist the producers of Canada. I remember distinctly the right hon. gentleman's declaration: "To her products I pledge my patronage, and to the cause of her producers I pledge my devotion." I am urging upon him the cause of the producers of Canada, particularly the fishermen, who at the present time are allowed to bring in rope free and who are now struck by this one per

cent excise tax on the one hand, having at the same time on the other to meet additional competition from fish coming in from Newfoundland. I submit to him that this is one instance in which the principle of assisting the primary producer should be carried into practice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman did not intend to suggest that we were now striking a blow at the fishing industry, because we have not changed the law as it stood. The Canadian fisherman has always been subject, since 1907, to competition with Newfoundland, and he still is. How has he been Struck?

He has to pay an excise tax of one per cent on the rope which he imports, and which is his raw material. The general law of Canada provides that all imports shall be subject to a one per cent excise tax, while the import which competes with him is exempt from that tax. And yet the raw material which he uses is to be taxed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Fish does not compete with beef. This is a case of fish, and in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick the fisherman stands in the same position to-day as he did before with respect to Newfoundland fish.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Absolutely the same
position. He is subject to the same competition, and by no specious argument can the hon. gentleman get away from that fact. The putting of a duty of one cent on a pair of scales does not change the question of competition of Newfoundland with New Brunswick and Nova Scotia fish. Section 17 of the Newfoundland customs tariff reads:
Provided always that the governor in council may, at any time when it shall be made to appear to him to he for the interest of the colony, by proclamation to be published in the Newfoundland Gazette, suspend the operation of this clause for a limited period, the duration of the said period to be stated in the said proclamation, in respect of all or any of the above mentioned articles.
This covers such items as flour, pork and so on, which now go from this country to the colony of Newfoundland. A convention has been maintained for many years which provides that our products shall be permitted to enter Newfoundland free of duty and that we are not to put imposts against their fish coming into this country.

I submit that there is no convention to prevent the imposition of an excise duty.

Special War Revenue Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Newfoundland legislature did not limit it to customs duty. This matter has been crystallized into the form of a convention by which our exports go into Newfoundland free of duty and their fish comes into this country free of duty. This procedure has been enforced by statute since 1907, with the limitation that we might at any time by proclamation make their products subject to our duty. The hon. member this afternoon admitted, very properly, I think, that we might put the government of Newfoundland in a position where they might issue a proclamation. Such action would be undesirable; the loss to the country as a whole would be greater than any benefits which might accrue. If our fishermen were being subjected to greater competition than they have had to meet heretofore, the position would be different. The competition remains the same; there has been no change, and no change is contemplated. Newfoundland fish came in free, they will continue to come in free; our exports found a market in Newfoundland by reason of the convention to which I have referred, and they will continue to do so.
It is true that the impost of one per cent applies to rope, but it will be noticed that this will amount to only one dollar for $100 worth, and $10 for $1,000 worth. That is the only impost with respect to rope, as this article will be free from the sales tax. I do not think any fisherman will raise a question as to the payment of that small tax.

The right hon. the Minister of Finance made that same argument this afternoon, that no fisherman or no citizen of Canada would object to paying this tax. He seems to have the idea that the only tax paid by the people of this country is the stamp tax and the special taxes included in this resolution. If the people of the Dominion of Canada will look at their dinner plates or at their clothes they will soon see the taxes they are paying to this country. It does not need a one per cent excise tax or a Stamp on cheques to convince them that they are paying their share to assist what my right hon. friend describes as a national emergency.
I submit that the fishing industry is being discriminated against as compared with the other primary producers. If there is any import which competes with the farmer, he is protected to the extent of the imposition of the one per cent excise tax. In the case of the lumberman, pulpwood coming in from Newfoundland is subject to the one per cent excise tax. If anything is imported which competes in any way with the miner, the
same tax is imposed. But in the case of the fisherman the one per cent excise tax is taken off and at the same time a tax is imposed upon his tools of trade. The fisherman is left exposed to this competition, and I submit that in order to be able to meet it he should be compensated by receiving exemption on the articles used in his trade. My right hon. friend may not know it, but it costs these men $700, $800 or $1,000 per season to fit out, and no small part of that amount is made up in the purchase of rope. I have asked my right hon. friend time and time again to try to see my point of view, namely, that the fisherman is exposed to competition which is not open to any other primary producer, and at the same time he has to pay this additional tax. I do not intend to delay the committee, but I submit that the convention can easily be overcome. If the excise tax can be excepted in the case of Newfoundland fish, then it can be excepted in the case of the rope which is used by the fishermen of Canada in connection with their fishing operations.

Would the Minister of
Finance advise the committee if clause 14 on page 2 of the bill applies to mutual fire insurance companies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not in this bill.

I confess I cannot understand why this one per cent tax is called an excise tax. It looks to me very much like a straight customs duty. Under the new rates many articles will carry a duty of 100 per cent, and that would mean not a one per cent excise tax, but a two per cent tax to be levied on the real value of the goods, because this tax is levied on the duty paid value. There is a considerable list of exemptions, and I should like to know upon what basis the Minister of Finance determined what articles should be exempt. I see that split peas, barley meal, pot barley and vegetable plants are exempt. Upon what basis did the Minister of Finance select that list?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is the hon. member referring to the sales or excise tax?
Excise tax.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The excise tax is section 88.

That is the one to which
I am referring, the one per cent excise tax.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: That is a very limited list. It virtually means that the free list is abolished. There is practically nothing except a few things that would come in duty free, and the tax will work out in a great many cases to two per cent and not one per cent, which is equivalent to another increase in the tariff additional to the increases embodied in the budget, and without any justification. I would ask the minister why he calls this an excise tax?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Because it is.
In what respect?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is just what it says. It is a duty of one per cent imposed on the value of all goods brought into the country.

Collected by customs
officials?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: By whatever officials may be designated for the purpose, but presumably by the customs officials, although the excise department takes credit for it and it will appear in their returns.
Wherein does it differ from a customs duty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The duties of the customs tariff are either specfic or ad valorem duties or both, and some articles come in free. This has nothing to do with a customs tariff at all. It is a straight excise tax on all importations.

The 'minister's explanation
has not been explained yet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no explanation
beyond the fact that the tax is imposed to raise revenue at this time.

It is an excise tax because
you call it so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I draw the
attention again of my right hon. friend to what I think is going to be the effect of this tax on the export trade of Canada. In the first place it is a tax on all imports coming into Canada. The imports coming into Canada to-day may broadly be classified in three groups: commodities in the nature of necessaries of life; luxuries; or something that enters into some line of manufacturing or the development of the primary industries, either raw materials or implements of production. In other words, they are all, except luxuries, articles that enter into either the cost of living or the cost of production. They are coming in, that is to say being imported, for the simple reason that our people can obtain them by importing them at less cost than they could obtain them if obliged to pay for them when bought in Canada. On these goods is being placed a duty of one per cent. That duty is being imposed on the duty paid value of the goods imported, which will make the tax higher than appears on the face of it. That means with respect to all of our export trade, whether it arises from the primary industries-fishing, lumbering, mining, or any branch of	agricultureor from the secondary manufacturing industries, that those engaged in the export trade will have to the extent of more than one per cent on imported materials, tools and implements, and imported necessaries consumed by workers in industry, an additional burden of taxation to bear, and that will have to be carried notwithstanding that the only place where these surplus commodities can be sold is in world markets, which are the most competitive of all markets. I repeat that in world markets one or two per cent additional taxation placed upon those who are engaged in any branch of exportation, whether in the primary or in the manufacturing industries, may be just sufficient to cause the country to

Special War Revenue Act
lose its market abroad. While my right hon. friend may think he is going to get additional revenue in that way, I am afraid that what he will gain in one way, he will more than lose in export trade. What those engaged as producers or manufacturers in our export trade will lose will cost him and the coiuntTy very much more in the long run than all he will raise by this proposed taxation.

Take the case of raw
material coming in for the manufacture of binder twine. If the binder twine is consumed in Canada by the farmer, we pay the one per cent tax, but if exported the tax is not paid. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perfectly correct.
Is that fair?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I notice that raw leaf
tobacco when imported by a licenced tobacco or cigar manufacturer is exempt. We have a considerable tobacco industry coming along in our part of Ontario, and I was just wondering if the finance minister had considered every phase of this question and assured himself that there would be no injustice done to the growers of tobacco in Ontario.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know whether
my right hon. friend has observed that the new section 94 of the bill provides for a drawback of 99 per cent of all the excise tax that has been paid on goods that are exported. It used to be a drawback of 99 per cent of the consumption or sales tax applied in respect of materials used, but now we are providing for a drawback of 99 per cent with respect to any good used for export.

I wish to call the attention of the Prime Minister to a definition of excise. I always understood that an excise tax commonly meant a tax imposed within the country itself. Just for the information of the house I should like to give this dictionary definition of excise:
An inland duty or. impost levied upon the manufacture, sale or consumption of commodities within the country.
That is what this is.

Manufactured within the
country? I hardly understand how that could be applied to goods coming in from outside. To prevent misunderstanding I think it would be better to call this tax by another name.
By its own name, a tariff.

I do not want to delay the
committee, but I think there is a clause here
which really requires' explanation from the Prime Minister. Now that we have the Prime Minister here I trust that he will see to it that it is at least clarified. Item 704 covers:
Apparel, wearing and other personal and household effects, not merchandise, of British subjects dying abroad, but domiciled in Canada.
This afternoon we had from the Prime Minister a definition of domicile. It was the residence of a gentleman residing in a country and intending to reside there. It is true that this country may become a veritable paradise if the right hon. gentleman continues in power much longer, but at the same time the poor dead man has no chance. He has to go somewhere else, and if he is dead I doubt very much whether he can really be domiciled in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With my hon. friend's fund of information and knowledge of law he must know that every man has a domicile. As Lord Haldane said in the Jeffries case, a man's place of birth is his domicile of origin. He may lose that domicile of origin, and if there come a time when he no longer has a domicile he reverts to his domicile of origin. Every man who dies has at the time of his death a domicile.
Where is his animus re-vertendi?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The case in point is the Widener case in the House of Lords, with which I have no doubt my hon. friend in the course of his reading has become familiar. The person in question had lived for about twenty years in England, but the animus as expressed from time to time by his speeches was that he always looked upon the United States as his country; in other words he had given expression to an animus revertendi, a desire to return to his native land. The House of Lords decided that the United States was his domicile. The matter before us is not quite the joke that it might seem to be; every man who dies has a domicile either of origin or of choice.
If my right hon. friend had expressed it, "whose domicile previous to his death was in Canada," the statute would have been more properly drawn.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I quite agree, but my hon. friend will realize that the statute to which attention is now being directed mentions only a section of the Customs Act which existed for many years in its present form. All we have said is that the excise tax shall not apply to the provisions of that section, so that the wearing apparel and personal
Special War Revenue Act

effects of the deceased who is domiciled in Canada shall not be subject to the tax. No doubt my hon. friend with his ready wit thought this was a fit occasion for an enjoyable joke at the close of a difficult and hot session. On further consideration, however, he will realize that this is merely the mention of a section with the draftsmanship of which we are not at the moment concerned.
I do not ascribe to my right hon. friend the drafting of this section. But why exempt the wearing apparel of the dead man when the poor live man has to pay? Is there any reason for that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps the real reason lies in the difference between the government and the opposition.
The government, being itself on the verge of disillusionment, has great sympathy with dead men.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no.

The Prime Minister drew attention to the proposed section No. 94, and the right hon. leader of the opposition pointed out that the exporting industries of the country were to be prejudiced by the imposition of a one per cent special import tax. The Prime Minister's answer was that under the proposed section 94 a drawback of 99 per cent of that tax would be allowed. But section 94 is of no help whatever to those industries which export natural products.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so.
I do not think it is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. There would be no importations in the instance referred to by my hon. friend.
Yes, there are importations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The section reads:
.... paid in respect of materials used, wrought into or attached to articles exported, may be granted; provided that payment of a specific sums in lieu of such drawback may be authorized by the governor in council ....

In this connection I wish to mention an industry in the province of Nova Scotia which makes use of at least three classes of raw material or implements of production which have to be imported. First, fertilizers, which are brought in from Europe and the United States; second, spraying and dusting materials, a large proportion of which are brought in from abroad; third, spraying and dusting machines and apple grading machines, most of which are brought in from abroad. These machines are imported because

the imported products seem to be more suitable than the type produced in Canada. The proposal of the government is to place upon all these machines and the raw materials connected with the industry an additional import tax of one per cent. That industry cannot in any way be compensated by drawbacks. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think Mr. Chairman, that the returns asked for have been brought down. I regret I was not present the other evening when this matter was under consideration. It is only fair to say that it originated in the Department of External Affairs and not in the Department of Trade and Commerce. I have already indicated to the house the circumstances under which Sir Josiah Stamp was asked to become chairman of the commission. The grain trade selected Mr. Sanford Evans as its representative on the commission, and the Hon. Chief Justice Brown became the representative of the agrarian interests. As is indicated by the return filed to-day, Mr. Pearson of the Department of External Affairs was selected to act as secretary.
When the commission had concluded its labours Mr. Pearson returned to Ottawa and Mr. Sanford Evans also came here. Each of the commissioners had a copy of the evidence. The report had been drafted only, and it had been agreed that as Sir Josiah Stamp could stay in this country only a limited number of days, the typewriting of portions of the report that he had indicated, apart from what he had written, should be completed, and the report would be set up in type and mailed to him on the Mauretania, sailing on the succeeding Tuesday, so he might be able to revise and return the report to Canada. Mr. Pearson undertook the overseeing of that work. At the time among the appendices was the number 12 which had been put in evidence by Mr. Pitblado practically at the conclusion of the hearing, under the circumstances mentioned by him in his telegram.
I said the other day, and I now repeat in passing, that the real objection to that appendix was the red ink statement which drew inferences from the chart itself. I knew nothing of this, neither did anyone in the department so far as that is concerned. The report came back from London, approved by Sir Josiah Stamp. There were one of two typographical errors that he had corrected. But recall this, if you please, there were no appendices sent to Sir Josiah Stamp with the report.
When the report was returned, Mr. Pearson -a competent young man who has long been in the department and enjoys the confidence

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
of his superiors-sent the draft to the printing office, had it printed, and included with the appendices the appendix in question. I am informed that this was done in the ordinary course, it being believed that this was one of the appendices that should be attached. I am informed by Mr. Pearson that some little conversation took place between him and Mr. Evans, Mr. Evans believing that the appendix should be included as part of the report, and Mr. Pearson, as secretary, concurring in the suggestion of the commissioner because the appendix had been put in evidence at the hearing It is an elementary rule that any document put in in evidence may be printed as part of the report and the proceedings. This appendix was so included.
I	tabled the report. I notice it is suggested that it was my duty to read the report. I think not. The report was made to me by the commission, and it was my duty to table the report as I received it, without making any comment on it in any way, shape or form; which I did. Some days later I was called up by telephone asking if I had observed that the appendix had been included in the report to which exception had been taken by certain of the grain interests. I said the matter was entirely new to me because as a matter of fact I had not read the appendix. I immediately got the report and looked at the appendix. Then I went down to the office and inquired into the circumstances under which the appendix had been included in the report, with the results that I have just given to the committee.
I believe that the appendix would not have been received by a judge in a court of law if attention had been directed to the inferences drawn from it and which are printed in red. So far as the appendix itself is concerned, we would say that it could be put in evidence just for what it is worth. The inferences to be drawn would be left entirely to the commission itself rather than to the person who prepared the return. I understand the return was prepared by the statistical agency in Winnipeg of which Mr. Evans is the head. I am only told that; it does not appear so from the report.
There is nothing further that I can add. The copy of the evidence and the other documents were lodged in the department by Mr. Pearson in his capacity as secretary of the commission; they were not so lodged as a part of the files of the department. The documents are still in the department. I do not think the correspondence which took place is any part of the departmental correspon-

dence, I not having written any communication then in respect to it. As I have said, the communications which took place between the chairman, the members of the commission and the unfortunate secretary are in no sense part of the records of the department over which I can in any sense have control, and I do not regard them as such. I regret more than I can say that these difficulties arose, but they would have arisen in spite of any supervision which might have been made, because Sir Josiah Stamp indicated when he came to Canada that it was absolutely necessary for him to leave on a certain date by a certain ship. The inclusion of the appendix as a part of the report is in no sense objectionable either as a matter of evidence or fair dealing or as a matter of good faith between the commission and the department from which the commission issued. But, as I stated when my attention was directed to it by the hon. member for Humboldt, in my opinion the red printing which drew inferences from the document should not have appeared.
I issued instructions that the appendix should foe removed from all copies of the report in the department, and Mr. Pearson saw that the appendix was in fact removed. Those which have been circulated since that time have not contained that appendix. A certain number of copies, as indicated by the return filed to-day, have been issued to public libraries and to individuals who have asked for them; the Winnipeg Grain Exchange printed a certain number of copies of the evidence and obtained a number of copies of the report as well. From those copies of the report the appendix in question has been removed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to question in the least the accuracy of any statement made by my right hon. friend, but I hope he will not judge me too severely if I am a little critical of one aspect of what he has just said. The Prime Minister said it was his duty to present the report to this house just as it was received, without reading the report in the first instance himself or having anyone read it on his behalf.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was read in the department, of course.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not agree with the Prime Minister in that statement; I think he is responsible for the report being presented at all. His responsibility goes the length of his being obliged either to table the report and allow matters to develop as they may as a result of his so doing, or to

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
withhold the report either temporarily or permanently and give to parliament his reason for so doing.
I just wish to illustrate where the failure of appreciating that circumstance has led my right hon. friend. He has brought into the discussion to-night the name of a member of the civil service who is not in a position to make any statement in his own behalf.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the right hon. gentleman will pardon me, I did not bring his name into this matter until it had been brought in through the report filed, in which he desired his name should be put as secretary of the commission.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That does not matter in the least; I wish to make a very clear statement about the position and rights of members of the civil service of this country. It is a rule of parliamentary practice and procedure that members of the civil service who are not in a position to answer for themselves or to make statements on their own behalf should be protected from having their names mentioned in discussion on the floor of parliament by any minister or any member of this house unless they are being criticized personally for some act for which they must take the full responsibility. My right hon. friend would have been perfectly within his rights had he said that all this was due to the fact that a member of his staff, or a member of the public service, had inserted this chart without his knowledge, that he regretted the circumstances though prepared to take responsibility for it. The responsibility would necessarily be his for not having observed that the chart which should not have been inserted had been placed there. He cannot escape that responsibility.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What nonsense.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is not nonsense; I take distinct issue with my right hon. friend, and I think we might as well have the difference understood at once.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, let us talk it right
out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think I
approached this matter in a courteous way; I hope to proceed in the same manner, and I ask the Prime Minister to extend a like courtesy to me during my statement. I say, on behalf of the civil service of Canada, that the Prime Minister of any country has no right to bring in, by way of excuse for any action of the government, the name of any member of the civil service. That is a fundamental rule of, parliamentary practice and
procedure, and if the Prime Minister has not known it up to the present he had better follow it hereafter. The public service is entitled to all the protection parliament can throw around its members; if individual members seek to do their duty faithfully and well they are entitled to the protection of every hon. member of this house, of the government, and most of all of the Prime Minister. I say it is an entire breach of what is right and proper that Mr. Pearson's name should have been mentioned at all by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister should have taken full responsibility and should have said quite frankly, as he is quite capable of doing, that the fault was that of the department of which he is the head and for which he is responsible. He must take responsibility if an error is committed, and he has no right, by way of escape of censure, to bring the name of a public servant into the discussion at all.
May I say that I do not think this error of mentioning the name of a civil servant and holding him responsible would have been committed if my right hon. friend had taken the true view of his responsibility as a minister of the crown. He is responsible for every act of the department over which he presides, just as other ministers are responsible for the acts of their departments. A minister cannot escape responsibility, and it is not at all necessary for a minister to lay any document on the table of the house without so much as having read it or of having others read it in the first instance. The first duty of the government is to peruse every document coming before it and decide whether or not the document is to be made public. If there is an order of the house calling for the production of documents the ministry exercise the right, which in fact its members have been exercising all along this session, of saying documents are not in a form in which they cam be presented to parliament, and that they cannot be produced except on an order of the house. I do submit that my right hon. friend should be more careful about bringing in the names of members of the public service. I am not saying this in a critical way, but I do feel it my duty to the public service of Canada to assert the principle I have, so that an error of this kind may not be repeated.
Mr. B'ENNETT: Mr. Chairman, the name of Mr. Pearson was brought into this matter in consequence of a colleague of the right hon. gentleman, the ex-Minister of Agriculture, asking who was the secretary of the commission.
